questions.question: A 55-year-old with stable uncomplicated hypertension exercises little, drinks 180 g of alcohol weekly and uses ibuprofen most days for knee pain. Which plan best fits ESC 2024 lifestyle advice and contributor review?
options: Build toward 75 minutes/week of vigorous activity, reduce alcohol and substitute scheduled naproxen
Build toward 75 minutes/week of moderate aerobic activity, maintain alcohol and review NSAID use
Build toward 150 minutes/week of moderate aerobic activity, maintain alcohol and continue scheduled ibuprofen
Build toward 150 minutes/week of moderate aerobic activity, reduce alcohol and review NSAID use
questions.explanation:
Exercise and Reversible Contributors to Poor BP Control

Correct answer: Build toward 150 minutes/week of moderate aerobic activity, reduce alcohol and review NSAID use

Physical Activity and Alcohol

**A practical ESC aerobic goal is at least 150 minutes of moderate activity weekly or 75 minutes of vigorous activity.** Add suitable low-to-moderate intensity resistance exercise on two to three days per week.

Progress gradually from the patient’s current activity and joint limitations; walking, cycling or other tolerable activities can be selected. Unstable cardiovascular symptoms or severe uncontrolled disease require assessment before vigorous training.

Alcohol intake of ==180 g/week== exceeds the ESC upper limit of about ==100 g/week== of pure alcohol. Counsel reduction, explain local drink sizes and avoid treating the upper limit as a recommended intake. Assess dependence and withdrawal risk when planning reduction in a heavy drinker.

Medication and Sleep Review

**Regular NSAIDs can worsen BP control through renal prostaglandin inhibition and sodium retention.** They can also blunt antihypertensive responses and increase kidney risk, especially with a diuretic plus ACE inhibitor or ARB.

Review whether ibuprofen can be reduced or replaced with a clinically appropriate pain strategy; do not assume that another nonselective oral NSAID removes the class effect. Check kidney function and electrolytes when the exposure and regimen warrant it.

Ask about sympathomimetic decongestants, stimulants, glucocorticoids, liquorice-containing products and other relevant exposures. Screen for OSA when snoring, witnessed apneas, daytime sleepiness or resistant hypertension suggests it. Sleep treatment and exercise complement indicated medicines rather than automatically replacing them. A diary of home BP and exposure changes can help assess response. Labeling hypertension resistant before assessing adherence, out-of-office measurements and these reversible factors risks unnecessary escalation. Avoid advising an abrupt unsupervised alcohol withdrawal if there is a history suggesting physiological dependence.

Build toward 75 minutes/week of vigorous activity, reduce alcohol and substitute scheduled naproxen: The exercise and alcohol components are reasonable. Naproxen may be selected for particular analgesic circumstances, but it remains an NSAID and does not remove the need to review drug-related BP elevation and kidney risk.

Build toward 75 minutes/week of moderate aerobic activity, maintain alcohol and review NSAID use: Seventy-five minutes can be an alternative weekly target for vigorous activity, not the usual moderate-intensity target. The substantial alcohol intake also warrants reduction rather than being left unchanged.

questions.explanationHtml:
Exercise and Reversible Contributors to Poor BP Control

Correct answer: D — Build toward 150 minutes/week of moderate aerobic activity, reduce alcohol and review NSAID use

Physical Activity and Alcohol

  • A practical ESC aerobic goal is at least 150 minutes of moderate activity weekly or 75 minutes of vigorous activity. Add suitable low-to-moderate intensity resistance exercise on two to three days per week.
    • Progress gradually from the patient’s current activity and joint limitations; walking, cycling or other tolerable activities can be selected. Unstable cardiovascular symptoms or severe uncontrolled disease require assessment before vigorous training.
    • Alcohol intake of 180 g/week exceeds the ESC upper limit of about 100 g/week of pure alcohol. Counsel reduction, explain local drink sizes and avoid treating the upper limit as a recommended intake. Assess dependence and withdrawal risk when planning reduction in a heavy drinker.

Medication and Sleep Review

  • Regular NSAIDs can worsen BP control through renal prostaglandin inhibition and sodium retention. They can also blunt antihypertensive responses and increase kidney risk, especially with a diuretic plus ACE inhibitor or ARB.
    • Review whether ibuprofen can be reduced or replaced with a clinically appropriate pain strategy; do not assume that another nonselective oral NSAID removes the class effect. Check kidney function and electrolytes when the exposure and regimen warrant it.
    • Ask about sympathomimetic decongestants, stimulants, glucocorticoids, liquorice-containing products and other relevant exposures. Screen for OSA when snoring, witnessed apneas, daytime sleepiness or resistant hypertension suggests it. Sleep treatment and exercise complement indicated medicines rather than automatically replacing them. A diary of home BP and exposure changes can help assess response. Labeling hypertension resistant before assessing adherence, out-of-office measurements and these reversible factors risks unnecessary escalation. Avoid advising an abrupt unsupervised alcohol withdrawal if there is a history suggesting physiological dependence.

Naproxen may be selected for particular analgesic circumstances, but it remains an NSAID and does not remove the need to review drug-related BP elevation and kidney risk.
  • B — Build toward 75 minutes/week of moderate aerobic activity, maintain alcohol and review NSAID use: Seventy-five minutes can be an alternative weekly target for vigorous activity, not the usual moderate-intensity target. The substantial alcohol intake also warrants reduction rather than being left unchanged.
  • C — Build toward 150 minutes/week of moderate aerobic activity, maintain alcohol and continue scheduled ibuprofen: The exercise component is appropriate, but it does not neutralize alcohol-related pressure elevation or the potential renal and sodium-retaining effects of regular NSAID exposure.

questions.question: A 54-year-old has confirmed untreated BP averaging 158/96 mmHg. Kidney function and potassium are normal; there is no heart failure, coronary disease or arrhythmia. Under AHA/ACC 2025, which initial regimen is preferred among these options?
options: An ARB plus a beta blocker in separate tablets
An ARB alone, with the second agent deferred until maximal-dose failure
An ARB plus a long-acting dihydropyridine CCB in a single tablet
An ACE inhibitor plus diltiazem in separate tablets
questions.explanation:
Initial Combination Therapy in Stage 2 Hypertension

Correct answer: An ARB plus a long-acting dihydropyridine CCB in a single tablet

Treatment Selection

**AHA/ACC 2025 favors two first-line agents from different classes for stage-two hypertension, preferably in a single-pill combination.** The ARB and dihydropyridine CCB address complementary mechanisms and are an appropriate pair in this uncomplicated patient.

Other appropriate foundational combinations include an ACE inhibitor or ARB with a thiazide-type diuretic. The stem asks for the best listed option; it does not imply that an ARB–CCB combination is superior in every patient.

Single-pill combinations reduce pill burden and can improve adherence, but the selected strengths must suit the individual. A combination containing two renin–angiotensin blockers is not an acceptable interpretation of complementary therapy.

Doses and Monitoring

**Start with suitable doses and titrate against standardized office and home readings.** Illustrative adult doses are losartan ==50 mg== once daily, increased to ==100 mg== daily when appropriate, and amlodipine ==5 mg== once daily, increased to ==10 mg== daily.

Selected frail, small, elderly or hepatically impaired adults may need amlodipine ==2.5 mg== initially. Product availability and fixed-dose strengths vary, so confirm the actual preparation rather than treating a generic example as a prescription for every patient.

Check baseline creatinine and potassium before ARB treatment and recheck after initiation or dose changes, earlier if renal or volume-related risk is high. Monitor ankle edema with amlodipine, postural symptoms and adherence. Continue lifestyle treatment and review the response during titration. Pregnancy requires a different drug choice because ACE inhibitors and ARBs can harm the fetus. Confirming stage two is a chronic-treatment decision; the absence of acute organ injury means this pressure alone does not require intravenous treatment or immediate normalization.

An ARB plus a beta blocker in separate tablets: This combination can fit a patient with an additional beta-blocker indication, such as angina, HFrEF or a rate-control requirement. No such indication is supplied; a first-line complementary pair and a single-pill format are preferred here.

An ARB alone, with the second agent deferred until maximal-dose failure: Monotherapy can be reasonable for selected stage-one patients or when tolerance calls for cautious initiation. Stage-two hypertension usually benefits from starting two complementary first-line drugs rather than a prolonged sequential monotherapy trial.

An ACE inhibitor plus diltiazem in separate tablets: This pair can lower BP and may suit selected patients needing angina or rate-control treatment. Without such an indication, the usual first-line CCB component is a long-acting dihydropyridine; the single-pill ARB–dihydropyridine pair is the preferred listed starting strategy.

questions.question: Despite confirmed adherence to losartan 100 mg and amlodipine 10 mg daily, a patient has home BP averaging 148/92 mmHg. eGFR is 78 mL/min/1.73 m² and potassium 4.1 mmol/L. Which addition best completes the usual foundational three-drug regimen?
options: Enalapril 10 mg daily
Chlorthalidone 12.5 mg daily
Doxazosin modified release 4 mg daily
Diltiazem extended release 120 mg daily
questions.explanation:
Complementary Triple Therapy and Dual Renin–Angiotensin Blockade

Correct answer: Chlorthalidone 12.5 mg daily

Foundational Combination

**The usual three-drug framework is one ACE inhibitor or ARB, a long-acting dihydropyridine CCB and an appropriate diuretic.** Losartan and amlodipine supply the first two components; chlorthalidone supplies the missing natriuretic mechanism.

A common low starting dose is ==12.5 mg== once daily, with subsequent titration according to pressure, electrolytes, renal function and tolerance. Lower doses or slower titration may be appropriate in vulnerable patients.

Thiazide-like agents such as chlorthalidone or indapamide provide sustained action. Selection still depends on local availability, the individual response and adverse effects rather than a rule that all patients must take one named diuretic.

Adverse Effects and Monitoring

**Check sodium, potassium and kidney function after starting or increasing the diuretic.** Hypokalemia, hyponatremia, volume depletion and a rise in uric acid are important dose-limiting effects.

Review gout, previous severe thiazide-associated hyponatremia, orthostatic symptoms and interacting medicines. A normal baseline potassium does not eliminate the need for follow-up.

Do not add an ACE inhibitor to the ARB to chase a lower pressure or a lower urine albumin result. Dual blockade can increase acute kidney injury and hyperkalemia, especially during dehydration or NSAID exposure. A beta blocker, alpha blocker or other later-line agent may eventually be appropriate for a specific indication, but the missing basic regimen should be addressed first. If pressure remains high on the completed regimen, confirm out-of-office elevation, tolerated doses and adherence before calling it true resistant hypertension. This question therefore tests treatment sequencing rather than simply identifying another drug capable of lowering BP.

Enalapril 10 mg daily: An ACE inhibitor can replace an ARB for an appropriate reason, but adding one to a full-dose ARB creates dual renin–angiotensin blockade. Extra blockade increases renal and potassium-related harm without being the recommended route to routine BP control.

Doxazosin modified release 4 mg daily: An alpha blocker can be used later, particularly with coexisting lower urinary tract symptoms or when preferred drugs cannot be used. The patient has not yet received the diuretic component of the foundational regimen.

Diltiazem extended release 120 mg daily: Diltiazem can be useful for angina or rate control in an appropriate patient. Adding a second CCB does not address sodium retention as directly as the missing thiazide-like diuretic and adds a separate heart-rate and conduction effect.

questions.question: A patient with hypertension and established coronary disease remains symptomatic with predictable exertional angina on amlodipine 10 mg daily. BP is 148/88 mmHg, sinus rate 94/min and LVEF 60%. There is no rest angina, AV block or bronchospastic disease. Which listed add-on best addresses both BP and the elevated heart-rate component of myocardial demand?
options: Bisoprolol
Losartan
Indapamide
Doxazosin
questions.explanation:
Beta Blockade for Hypertension With Exertional Angina

Correct answer: Bisoprolol

Clinical Indication

**Exertional angina with a relatively high sinus rate provides an additional reason to select beta blockade for hypertension.** Slower heart rate and reduced contractility decrease myocardial oxygen demand, while a longer diastolic interval can improve the time available for coronary perfusion.

The patient remains symptomatic on a full usual amlodipine dose and has neither bradycardia nor important conduction disease. Adding a suitable beta blocker therefore addresses more than the office pressure.

The symptom phenotype matters. Suspected vasospastic angina requires a different approach, generally centered on calcium-channel blockade; nonselective beta blockade may aggravate spasm. Do not generalize this answer to every form of chest pain.

Treatment and Monitoring

**Begin an appropriate low dose and titrate against angina, heart rate, BP and tolerance.** Bisoprolol is commonly started at ==5 mg== once daily for hypertension, with a lower starting dose considered in selected vulnerable patients.

Review fatigue, symptomatic bradycardia, exercise intolerance and conduction abnormalities. Amlodipine can be combined with beta blockade, while adding verapamil or diltiazem requires much greater attention to additive AV-nodal depression.

Treat the coronary risk profile and assess persistent or changing ischemic symptoms rather than merely adjusting antihypertensive doses. Improvement in stable angina is not proof that long-term beta blockade reduces mortality in every patient with coronary disease and preserved EF. HFrEF supplies a separate outcome-based indication, for which bisoprolol, carvedilol and extended-release metoprolol succinate have specific evidence. In hypertension without an additional indication, the usual first-line classes remain ACE inhibitors or ARBs, long-acting dihydropyridine CCBs and thiazide-type drugs. Avoid abrupt withdrawal in a patient with coronary disease, because rebound sympathetic activity can worsen ischemia.

Losartan: An ARB can improve BP and may be particularly useful with albuminuric CKD or other indications. It does not directly slow sinus rate or reduce exercise-related demand through beta blockade, which is the additional treatment priority specified here.

Indapamide: A thiazide-like diuretic is an appropriate component of a BP regimen and may be needed later. It does not provide the direct heart-rate and contractility effects that make a beta blocker a better fit for the current angina phenotype.

Doxazosin: An alpha blocker can lower BP and may help concurrent prostatic symptoms. It is not an established demand-reducing antianginal choice and may produce orthostatic symptoms or reflex tachycardia.

Renin–Angiotensin Blockade in Albuminuric Diabetic CKD

Correct answer: Losartan 50 mg daily, with renal function and potassium monitoring

questions.question: A patient with stage 4 CKD and eGFR 23 mL/min/1.73 m² has persistent hypertension despite an ARB, amlodipine and an appropriately adjusted loop diuretic. Which statement about adding chlorthalidone is best supported by CLICK?
options: Its BP effect requires stopping the loop diuretic before initiation
It can lower ambulatory BP, with careful electrolyte and kidney monitoring
Its main demonstrated benefit was prevention of kidney failure requiring dialysis
Its BP effect is too small to be useful once eGFR is below 30
questions.explanation:
Chlorthalidone in Stage 4 CKD: The CLICK Trial

Correct answer: It can lower ambulatory BP, with careful electrolyte and kidney monitoring

Trial Population and Results

**CLICK tested chlorthalidone in advanced CKD with poorly controlled hypertension confirmed by ABPM.** It demonstrated that thiazide-like treatment can remain effective at filtration rates below ==30 mL/min/1.73 m²==.

The starting dose was ==12.5 mg== daily, with four-weekly escalation when needed to a maximum of ==50 mg== daily. The primary endpoint was the change in twenty-four-hour ambulatory systolic BP at twelve weeks.

The adjusted between-group difference in that endpoint was about ==10.5 mmHg== favoring chlorthalidone. This demonstrates BP efficacy in the enrolled population; it is not proof of mortality reduction or prevention of dialysis.

Combination Diuresis and Safety

**Monitor for hypokalemia, a reversible creatinine rise, dizziness, hyperuricemia and other metabolic effects.** Combining distal and loop diuretic action can increase natriuresis but also increases the risk of excessive volume removal.

Review baseline volume status, sodium, potassium, magnesium and renal function. Plan early reassessment and individualize the initial dose and loop regimen, particularly in a frail patient or one with orthostatic symptoms.

Low eGFR alone should not be used to declare chlorthalidone ineffective, but evidence of efficacy does not imply universal safety or automatic suitability. A loop diuretic remains useful for substantial volume overload in advanced CKD. Interpret this trial as supporting a selected add-on option within a monitored regimen. Before adding another drug, confirm adherence and out-of-office elevation and review sodium intake and other contributors. A large filtration change or electrolyte abnormality after initiation requires clinical reassessment rather than assuming that the trial makes such effects acceptable.

Its BP effect requires stopping the loop diuretic before initiation: Volume status and loop dose need review when combining diuretics, but CLICK included loop-diuretic users and stratified randomization by that exposure. Mandatory withdrawal was not the condition establishing benefit.

Its main demonstrated benefit was prevention of kidney failure requiring dialysis: The trial established short-term ambulatory BP lowering, not a definitive reduction in dialysis or long-term kidney-failure events. An albuminuria change should not be substituted for a proven hard renal outcome.

Its BP effect is too small to be useful once eGFR is below 30: This was a traditional assumption about thiazide efficacy. CLICK specifically studied stage 4 CKD and demonstrated meaningful BP lowering, while also documenting adverse effects requiring close monitoring.

CLICK: chlorthalidone in advanced CKD, 2021 — https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2110730

questions.question: Ten days after starting chlorthalidone, a 72-year-old develops nausea and unsteadiness. Sodium is 121 mmol/L, potassium 2.9 mmol/L, urine osmolality 420 mOsm/kg and urine sodium 68 mmol/L. Diet and fluid intake are unchanged. Which explanation is most likely?
options: Glucocorticoid deficiency with increased vasopressin activity
Primary polydipsia with appropriate renal water excretion
SIADH from an occult pulmonary disorder
Thiazide-associated hyponatremia with impaired urinary dilution
questions.explanation:
Thiazide-Associated Hyponatremia With SIADH-Like Findings

Correct answer: Thiazide-associated hyponatremia with impaired urinary dilution

Pathophysiology and Recognition

**Thiazides inhibit distal sodium chloride reabsorption at a cortical diluting segment while preserving the medullary concentrating mechanism.** Water excretion can therefore become impaired, particularly when other stimuli promote vasopressin activity.

Older age, low body mass, high water intake and interacting drugs can increase vulnerability. Hyponatremia may appear early after initiation but can also emerge later when a new illness or medication changes water balance.

The biochemical pattern can resemble SIADH, including concentrated urine and a relatively high urine sodium. Urine sodium is harder to interpret during active diuretic action; it should not by itself establish a separate primary SIADH diagnosis.

Treatment and Monitoring

**Stop the implicated thiazide and assess symptoms, volume status, chronicity and the sodium trajectory.** Check potassium, magnesium, renal function and other potential contributors.

Seizures, marked encephalopathy or other severe manifestations require monitored hypertonic-saline treatment according to a hyponatremia protocol. Mildly symptomatic or stable cases need a volume-appropriate plan rather than automatic hypertonic saline or indiscriminate isotonic fluid.

Correct potassium carefully because potassium replacement itself can raise serum sodium. Withdrawal of the drug and correction of volume depletion may restore water excretion rapidly, creating a risk of overcorrection; frequent sodium checks are essential in significant cases. Hypokalemia increases vulnerability to osmotic demyelination and requires a conservative correction plan. Review uric acid and gout because thiazides can also cause hyperuricemia. A previous severe thiazide-associated episode is an important warning against casual rechallenge. The immediate task is medication-related dysnatremia assessment, not simply replacing the drug with a higher-dose member of the same class.

Glucocorticoid deficiency with increased vasopressin activity: Adrenal insufficiency can impair water excretion and mimic SIADH, so cortisol assessment may be relevant when the presentation is unexplained. The temporal drug relationship and hypokalemia favor a thiazide effect in this stem.

Primary polydipsia with appropriate renal water excretion: Uncomplicated primary polydipsia generally produces very dilute urine when renal dilution is intact. The concentrated urine and new distal diuretic exposure point toward impaired water excretion rather than an isolated increase in water intake.

SIADH from an occult pulmonary disorder: SIADH can produce similar urine findings and apparent euvolemia, and a separate cause may need consideration if abnormalities persist. Recent thiazide exposure and potassium loss are a more immediate explanation; the diuretic also limits use of usual SIADH diagnostic criteria.

questions.topic: Initial drug selection and adverse effects
questions.question: Amlodipine was increased from 5 to 10 mg daily in a patient with hypertension. Bilateral evening ankle edema appears; lungs are clear, JVP is normal and kidney function is stable. BP remains 146/88 mmHg. Which adjustment best addresses the likely mechanism and BP control?
options: Replace amlodipine with an equivalent high dose of nifedipine
Maintain amlodipine 10 mg and add furosemide
Reduce amlodipine and add an appropriate ACE inhibitor or ARB
Maintain the current dose and use compression alone
questions.explanation:
Dihydropyridine CCB Edema and Treatment Adjustment

Correct answer: Reduce amlodipine and add an appropriate ACE inhibitor or ARB

Mechanism and Differential Diagnosis

**Dihydropyridine CCBs dilate precapillary arterioles more than postcapillary vessels.** The resulting rise in capillary hydrostatic pressure promotes dependent fluid movement despite the absence of generalized sodium retention.

Edema often increases with dose and is more evident after standing. Its appearance after amlodipine escalation, with normal JVP and clear lungs, supports the drug mechanism in this patient.

Still assess alternative explanations when the history or examination suggests them, including heart failure, kidney or liver disease and venous pathology. Unilateral painful swelling deserves a different evaluation.

Treatment Selection

**Reduce the offending dose, switch strategy if necessary and use a complementary agent when BP remains high.** An ACE inhibitor or ARB can improve the regimen and may lessen CCB-associated edema, although it does not guarantee complete resolution.

An illustrative adjustment is a return to amlodipine ==5 mg== daily with initiation of a suitable RAS blocker, selected using kidney function, potassium and other indications. Check creatinine and potassium after introducing or titrating that agent.

A loop diuretic should be reserved for an actual indication rather than used as a prescribing cascade for every swollen ankle. Monitor pressure and orthostatic symptoms after the change; two lower-dose complementary agents may be better tolerated than pushing one agent to its maximum. Do not use an ACE inhibitor or ARB in pregnancy. If edema persists or the diagnosis becomes uncertain, reassess rather than escalating diuresis automatically. The distinction from volume-overload edema explains both the treatment choice and why a normal lung examination alone would not be sufficient to dismiss edema in a patient with other evidence of heart failure.

Replace amlodipine with an equivalent high dose of nifedipine: Another dihydropyridine may lower BP, but the same class mechanism can reproduce ankle edema, especially at higher doses. A class substitution does not directly resolve the dose-related precapillary vasodilation problem.

Maintain amlodipine 10 mg and add furosemide: A loop diuretic is appropriate for genuine systemic volume overload, including selected heart-failure or kidney presentations. Isolated dose-related CCB edema is chiefly a capillary-pressure problem and may respond poorly to diuresis, which can instead deplete intravascular volume.

Maintain the current dose and use compression alone: Compression and leg elevation can provide symptomatic support when appropriate. They do not address the new dose-related adverse effect or the remaining above-target pressure as directly as a regimen adjustment with a complementary drug.

questions.question: Two weeks after starting lisinopril, creatinine rises from 1.20 to 1.65 mg/dL. The patient has had diarrhea, takes regular ibuprofen and is clinically volume depleted. Potassium is 5.1 mmol/L. What is the best immediate approach?
options: Withhold lisinopril temporarily, stop NSAID exposure, correct depletion and reassess renal function
Continue lisinopril unchanged and recheck creatinine at the routine three-month visit
Replace lisinopril with losartan at an equivalent BP-lowering dose
Arrange renal-artery imaging before changing medication or volume management
questions.explanation:
A Major Creatinine Rise After ACE Inhibitor Initiation

Correct answer: Withhold lisinopril temporarily, stop NSAID exposure, correct depletion and reassess renal function

Interpretation of the Renal Response

**ACE inhibition dilates the efferent arteriole and can produce an expected early fall in filtration.** The size, timing and clinical context determine whether that response can be accepted.

The increase from 1.20 to ==1.65 mg/dL== is 0.45/1.20 × 100, approximately ==37.5%==. KDIGO 2024 advises continuing ACE inhibitor or ARB therapy unless creatinine rises by more than ==30%== within four weeks after initiation or dose increase.

Crossing that threshold prompts evaluation; it is not proof of bilateral renal-artery stenosis and does not automatically establish permanent intolerance to the class.

Treatment and Reassessment

**Correct reversible causes of reduced renal perfusion and remove nephrotoxic contributors.** In this actively depleted patient, temporary ACE-inhibitor withholding, NSAID cessation and appropriate volume replacement are preferable to further RAS blockade.

Review diuretics, other potassium-retaining medicines, the BP trend and urine output. Repeat creatinine and potassium promptly according to the severity rather than waiting for a routine long-term visit.

If kidney function does not improve as expected, investigate additional causes including obstruction, intrinsic kidney injury or renovascular disease according to the phenotype. A large rise can occur with severe bilateral stenosis or stenosis affecting a solitary functioning kidney, but those are not the only explanations. Once the acute illness and laboratory abnormalities resolve, reconsider the original indication and a supervised restart with monitoring. This preserves potential cardiovascular and kidney benefit without treating an unsafe acute situation as a reason for indefinite continuation. The monitoring decision is based on the percentage change and clinical state, not whether the new creatinine remains within an approximate laboratory range.

Continue lisinopril unchanged and recheck creatinine at the routine three-month visit: A small stable hemodynamic creatinine increase may be acceptable with timely follow-up. Here the rise is about 38%, with active volume depletion and NSAID exposure, so waiting months would miss reversible kidney injury and potassium risk.

Replace lisinopril with losartan at an equivalent BP-lowering dose: An ARB can replace an ACE inhibitor for cough or another class-specific tolerability problem. Both alter glomerular efferent tone, so an immediate substitution does not remove the hemodynamic risk during depletion and NSAID exposure.

Arrange renal-artery imaging before changing medication or volume management: Renovascular disease is a consideration with a disproportionate filtration change, particularly when no reversible contributor explains it. The supplied dehydration and NSAID exposure require immediate correction; imaging should not postpone that assessment and treatment.

questions.question: A patient takes an ARB, amlodipine and chlorthalidone at tolerated doses. Repeated office BP is 162/94 mmHg, but validated home averages are 122/74 and ABPM averages 123/72 mmHg. There is no progressive organ damage or postural symptom. What is the best interpretation?
options: True resistant hypertension requiring a fourth drug
A treated white-coat effect rather than confirmed true resistant hypertension
Masked uncontrolled hypertension requiring a fourth drug
Sustained hypertension despite three drugs requiring diuretic escalation
questions.explanation:
Apparent Resistance and the Treated White-Coat Effect

Correct answer: A treated white-coat effect rather than confirmed true resistant hypertension

Diagnostic Requirements

**Apparent treatment-resistant hypertension is not the same as confirmed true resistance.** The latter requires an adequate complementary multidrug regimen, correct measurement, assessment of adherence and confirmation that pressure remains elevated outside the office.

In the American framework, resistance includes BP above goal despite three maximally tolerated complementary drugs, including a diuretic, or control that requires at least four drugs. The usual foundation is one ACE inhibitor or ARB, a long-acting CCB and a diuretic. A controlled patient on three drugs with an office-only elevation does not meet that definition.

White-coat effects, inaccurate technique, inadequate doses and nonadherence can mimic treatment failure. Check the actual drug list and whether the patient can obtain and take the medicines rather than assuming that a prescription proves exposure.

ABPM is particularly useful for office–home discordance. A validated home record also helps when collected with appropriate technique and enough readings; cuffless watch estimates should not replace reliable measurements.

Management and Monitoring

**Do not add a fourth drug solely to normalize the office number when out-of-office control is established.** Continue the appropriate regimen, lifestyle measures and longitudinal surveillance.

Discuss the discordance, standardize future office readings and reassess the home device and technique when needed. Avoid telling the patient to omit medication before clinic appointments to manipulate the reading.

Monitor for hypotension, kidney dysfunction and electrolyte effects according to the existing drugs. Repeat out-of-office assessment if the pattern changes, organ damage progresses or adherence becomes uncertain. A patient can transition from one phenotype to another, so the white-coat label is not permanent proof of control. Conversely, a markedly elevated office value with symptoms of acute organ injury still needs clinical assessment rather than automatic dismissal. In the stable patient described, the decision rests on two concordant reliable out-of-office methods, making reflex MRA initiation less defensible than recognition of pseudoresistance.

True resistant hypertension requiring a fourth drug: True resistance requires persistent out-of-office elevation after an adequate regimen, measurement quality and adherence are established. The supplied ambulatory and home averages do not confirm uncontrolled pressure.

Masked uncontrolled hypertension requiring a fourth drug: Masked uncontrolled hypertension has the reverse pattern: office measurements appear controlled while pressure outside the office is high. Both out-of-office methods here show control.

Sustained hypertension despite three drugs requiring diuretic escalation: Sustained uncontrolled pressure is elevated in both settings. Diuretic escalation can help genuine sodium-dependent resistance, but would risk excessive lowering when the reliable out-of-office pressure is already controlled.

questions.question: Adherence and sustained out-of-office hypertension are confirmed on losartan 100 mg, amlodipine 10 mg and hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg daily. eGFR is 82 mL/min/1.73 m², potassium 4.0 mmol/L and BP averages 150/92 mmHg. Which adjustment best optimizes the foundational regimen?
options: Replace hydrochlorothiazide with furosemide 40 mg daily
Add spironolactone while leaving the low-dose diuretic regimen unchanged
Add clonidine while leaving the current three drugs unchanged
Replace low-dose hydrochlorothiazide with an appropriately titrated thiazide-like diuretic
questions.explanation:
Diuretic Optimization Before Fourth-Line Treatment

Correct answer: Replace low-dose hydrochlorothiazide with an appropriately titrated thiazide-like diuretic

Treatment Sequencing

**Optimize drug exposure and the diuretic component before declaring resistance to an adequate triple regimen.** The ARB and CCB are at conventional full doses, while hydrochlorothiazide remains at a low dose.

Replacing it with chlorthalidone, often ==12.5 mg== daily initially and titrated as appropriate, or a suitable indapamide regimen can improve sustained pressure control. Increasing hydrochlorothiazide is another possible optimization strategy, although not the option offered here.

Account for dosing frequency, duration of action, adherence and the patient’s response. A drug’s presence on the list does not prove that its dose or pharmacological coverage is sufficient.

Safety and Subsequent Escalation

**Monitor sodium, potassium, renal function and standing symptoms after changing diuresis.** Longer action and greater potency can improve control but can also increase electrolyte or volume-related toxicity.

Review dietary sodium, regular NSAIDs, alcohol and other contributors. Assess secondary causes where indicated; changing the diuretic does not replace that evaluation.

If pressure remains high despite a tolerated optimized regimen, an MRA is an evidence-supported next option in a suitable renal and potassium setting. A loop diuretic is useful when the volume phenotype and kidney function favor it, not because every three-drug patient needs one. Chlorthalidone can still be effective in selected stage-four CKD patients, but those cases need a more cautious monitored plan than this patient with preserved filtration. The question tests the boundary between suboptimal treatment and failure of an adequate regimen, rather than claiming that one replacement drug guarantees control.

Replace hydrochlorothiazide with furosemide 40 mg daily: Loop diuretics are important for selected patients with volume overload or substantially reduced filtration. There is no such indication here; an appropriately dosed long-acting thiazide-like option better fits the usual foundational approach.

Add spironolactone while leaving the low-dose diuretic regimen unchanged: Spironolactone is a preferred fourth-line option once a suitable foundational triple regimen is optimized. The stem deliberately supplies a low-dose hydrochlorothiazide component, so review of diuretic strength and duration should precede labeling this as failure of optimal triple therapy.

Add clonidine while leaving the current three drugs unchanged: Clonidine can lower pressure in selected later-line settings, but sedation, adherence dependence and withdrawal hypertension make it a less attractive way to bypass optimization of the existing diuretic.

questions.question: A patient has confirmed adherent hypertension despite losartan 100 mg, amlodipine 10 mg and chlorthalidone 25 mg daily. Home BP averages 150/90 mmHg, eGFR is 74 mL/min/1.73 m² and potassium 4.0 mmol/L. Which add-on has the strongest PATHWAY-2 support?
options: Spironolactone 25 mg daily
Bisoprolol 5 mg daily
Doxazosin modified release 4 mg daily
Clonidine 0.1 mg twice daily
questions.explanation:
Fourth-Line Spironolactone and PATHWAY-2

Correct answer: Spironolactone 25 mg daily

Trial Evidence and Mechanism

**PATHWAY-2 supported spironolactone as the preferred add-on to an ACE inhibitor or ARB, CCB and diuretic in eligible resistant hypertension.** The randomized crossover trial compared spironolactone with placebo, bisoprolol and modified-release doxazosin.

Spironolactone was given at ==25–50 mg== daily. The principal evidence concerns home systolic BP lowering, not a trial-proven reduction in cardiovascular death compared with those alternatives.

Mineralocorticoid receptor blockade addresses sodium retention. A good response, particularly in a low-renin phenotype, does not by itself diagnose primary aldosteronism; diagnosis requires an appropriate biochemical and clinical assessment.

Eligibility and Monitoring

**Check kidney function and potassium before starting an MRA and shortly after initiation or titration.** The supplied eGFR and potassium are comfortably within the usual eligibility boundaries.

The 2025 American pathway has its strongest routine fourth-line evidence at eGFR at least ==45 mL/min/1.73 m²==. ESC 2024 allows selected use at eGFR at least 30 with potassium no more than ==4.5 mmol/L== and close monitoring. Do not silently substitute one society’s renal boundary for another.

Watch for hyperkalemia, a fall in filtration, breast tenderness, gynecomastia and menstrual effects. Risk increases with CKD, RAS blockade, potassium supplements and other potassium-retaining agents. Arrange an individualized early laboratory plan rather than waiting for annual blood tests. If the patient has an indication for primary-aldosteronism testing, consider the effect of starting an MRA on renin and aldosterone interpretation before treatment, while maintaining clinical safety. Evidence for BP lowering does not eliminate the need to evaluate secondary causes or confirm the foundational regimen.

ISH 2026 Qualification

**The ISH 2026 recommendation retains low-dose spironolactone as the preferred fourth drug after excluding pseudoresistance and optimizing diuretic-based therapy.** It specifies eGFR at least ==30 mL/min/1.73 m²== and potassium below ==4.5 mmol/L==, with close laboratory monitoring.

The strict potassium boundary in this named ISH recommendation should not be silently substituted for ESC wording or the higher renal threshold in the routine AHA 2025 pathway. The supplied potassium of ==4.0 mmol/L== and eGFR of 74 meet all three frameworks.

Later-Line Direct Vasodilators

**Minoxidil is a potent arteriolar vasodilator reserved for specialist-managed severe refractory hypertension.** It usually requires a loop diuretic for salt/water retention and a beta blocker or other sympathetic suppressant for reflex tachycardia.

The oral label starts at ==5 mg== daily in adults. Monitor weight, edema, heart rate, angina and possible pericardial effusion, which can progress to tamponade. Hypertrichosis is another characteristic adverse effect. Oral antihypertensive use must be distinguished from topical treatment for hair loss.

**Hydralazine is another later-line arteriolar dilator, with a different characteristic toxicity profile.** Reflex tachycardia and fluid retention can also require complementary treatment.

The US oral label starts at ==10 mg== four times daily for two to four days, then ==25 mg== four times daily for the remainder of the first week, with further individualized titration. Monitor for a lupus-like syndrome and other immune toxicity. This oral schedule is distinct from IV hydralazine used for an acute obstetric indication. Neither direct vasodilator substitutes for correcting pseudoresistance or optimizing the foundational regimen.

Evidence framework | Renal/potassium qualification

AHA/ACC 2025 routine fourth-line pathway | eGFR ==≥45 mL/min/1.73 m²==; assess potassium and monitor

ESC 2024 spironolactone guidance | eGFR ==≥30 mL/min/1.73 m²== and potassium ==≤4.5 mmol/L==

This patient | eGFR 74; potassium ==4.0 mmol/L==

Bisoprolol 5 mg daily: Bisoprolol is useful when beta blockade has an additional indication and was an active PATHWAY-2 comparator. Spironolactone produced a greater home systolic BP reduction in the studied resistant-hypertension population.

Doxazosin modified release 4 mg daily: Doxazosin can be useful later or with coexisting prostatic symptoms and was the other active PATHWAY-2 comparator. It was less effective than spironolactone for the trial’s BP endpoint.

Clonidine 0.1 mg twice daily: Clonidine can be a later-line antihypertensive but was not a PATHWAY-2 treatment arm. Its central adverse effects and withdrawal risk also matter when choosing a chronic fourth drug.

ESC 2024 spironolactone guidanceeGFR ≥30 mL/min/1.73 m² and potassium ≤4.5 mmol/L
This patienteGFR 74; potassium 4.0 mmol/L

  • C — Doxazosin modified release 4 mg daily: Doxazosin can be useful later or with coexisting prostatic symptoms and was the other active PATHWAY-2 comparator. It was less effective than spironolactone for the trial’s BP endpoint.
  • D — Clonidine 0.1 mg twice daily: Clonidine can be a later-line antihypertensive but was not a PATHWAY-2 treatment arm. Its central adverse effects and withdrawal risk also matter when choosing a chronic fourth drug.

questions.question: Spironolactone improves resistant hypertension but causes persistent painful gynecomastia. The patient has eGFR 78 mL/min/1.73 m², potassium 4.3 mmol/L and no diabetes, albuminuria or CYP3A-inhibiting drugs. The clinician plans to retain mineralocorticoid-receptor blockade for BP control. Which substitute best fits?
options: Eplerenone with potassium and kidney-function monitoring
Amiloride with potassium and kidney-function monitoring
Finerenone with potassium and kidney-function monitoring
Doxazosin with standing-pressure monitoring
questions.explanation:
Spironolactone Intolerance and Eplerenone

Correct answer: Eplerenone with potassium and kidney-function monitoring

Pharmacology and Selection

**Eplerenone is more selective for the mineralocorticoid receptor than spironolactone and has fewer sex-hormone-related adverse effects.** It is a reasonable steroidal MRA alternative when spironolactone-related gynecomastia limits treatment.

Lower antiandrogenic activity does not mean lower potassium risk. Both drugs reduce aldosterone-mediated potassium excretion, and concurrent ACE inhibitor or ARB therapy requires particular attention.

Do not use the post-MI HFrEF dose schedule as if it were the hypertension schedule. The US hypertension label starts eplerenone at ==50 mg== daily and allows escalation to ==50 mg== twice daily if the response is inadequate; resistant-hypertension regimens may use divided dosing.

Contraindications and Monitoring

**Measure potassium before treatment, within the first week and at one month after starting or changing the dose, then periodically.** Reassess earlier when illness or interacting medicines increase risk.

Strong CYP3A inhibitors are contraindicated. The US hypertension label additionally restricts use with creatinine clearance below ==50 mL/min==, type-two diabetes with microalbuminuria and certain other renal or potassium-related conditions; consult the indication-specific label.

A creatinine clearance threshold from the label is not numerically interchangeable with every eGFR-based guideline rule. Avoid overlapping potassium-sparing drugs or potassium supplementation unless a specialist plan specifically addresses the risks. The patient’s supplied profile avoids these major barriers, but laboratory follow-up remains necessary. If MRA therapy cannot be safely retained, a different mechanism such as amiloride or another later-line drug may be considered according to renal function and the clinical phenotype. The rationale for the selected substitution is preservation of useful aldosterone antagonism while reducing the particular adverse effect, not a guarantee of identical BP potency.

Newer Add-On Mechanisms and Safety

**Baxdrostat inhibits aldosterone synthesis rather than blocking the mineralocorticoid receptor.** Its 2026 US label permits add-on treatment for inadequately controlled adult hypertension; this does not establish approval in every country.

The labeled dose is ==2 mg== once daily, or ==1 mg== once daily when hyperkalemia or hyponatremia risk is increased. Correct potassium and sodium abnormalities before starting and monitor both periodically, more often in higher-risk patients.

Potassium-raising combinations require extra monitoring; strong or moderate CYP3A inducers can reduce treatment effect. The label lists no formal contraindications, which does not mean absence of clinically important risks. Drug-specific cardiovascular-event prevention has not been established in controlled outcome trials.

**Aprocitentan blocks ETA and ETB endothelin receptors and provides a different add-on mechanism.** The US dose is ==12.5 mg== once daily; the 25-mg trial dose is not the recommended dose.

Pregnancy and hypersensitivity are contraindications. Exclude pregnancy before treatment and use effective contraception during treatment and for one month after stopping. Monitor aminotransferases, bilirubin, hemoglobin, weight and fluid retention; edema and anemia are important adverse effects.

Avoid initiation with aminotransferases above three times the upper limit of normal or moderate-to-severe hepatic impairment. Significant fluid retention may require withdrawal; advanced or unstable heart failure limits suitability. Neither a newer mechanism nor a BP endpoint makes it an interchangeable first choice for this patient’s specific MRA-related gynecomastia.

Amiloride with potassium and kidney-function monitoring: Amiloride blocks the epithelial sodium channel and can be a useful alternative for selected resistant-hypertension patients. It does not retain mineralocorticoid receptor antagonism and still carries hyperkalemia risk.

Finerenone with potassium and kidney-function monitoring: Finerenone is a nonsteroidal MRA with specific cardiorenal evidence in eligible populations. It should not be assumed to provide interchangeable resistant-hypertension BP control or dosing evidence in a patient without those indications.

Doxazosin with standing-pressure monitoring: An alpha blocker can lower pressure and may help prostatic symptoms, but it abandons the sodium-retention-directed MRA mechanism. Orthostatic effects are also important, particularly during initiation.

questions.question: A patient taking clonidine 0.2 mg twice daily runs out of tablets. Thirty-six hours later there is headache, tremor, sweating and BP 196/112 mmHg with sinus tachycardia. Examination and initial testing show no acute target-organ injury. Which mechanism best explains the abrupt deterioration?
options: Mineralocorticoid excess from primary aldosteronism
Autonomous catecholamine secretion from a pheochromocytoma
Withdrawal of central alpha-2 agonism with sympathetic rebound
Thyroid-hormone excess causing increased adrenergic responsiveness
questions.explanation:
Clonidine Withdrawal and Rebound Hypertension

Correct answer: Withdrawal of central alpha-2 agonism with sympathetic rebound

Mechanism and Recognition

**Abrupt clonidine interruption removes central sympathetic suppression and can cause rebound hypertension.** Headache, agitation, tremor, sweating and tachycardia can accompany the rapid pressure rise.

A medication-supply history is therefore part of evaluating a hypertensive presentation. Ask about missed doses, vomiting, inability to obtain tablets and recent changes to centrally acting treatment.

The pressure number alone does not determine whether this is a hypertensive emergency. Assess for encephalopathy, focal deficits, acute coronary ischemia, pulmonary edema, aortic syndromes and acute kidney injury.

Treatment and Prevention

**Restore a supervised treatment plan and address the withdrawal mechanism while monitoring pressure and symptoms.** Reintroduction of clonidine can reverse rebound in an appropriate patient; acute organ injury would require an emergency-specific monitored approach.

Do not rely on isolated escalation of pure beta blockade to manage an unassessed withdrawal syndrome. The prescribing information warns that concurrent beta blockade can increase withdrawal risk.

For planned discontinuation, taper rather than stop abruptly. The oral label describes a gradual reduction over two to four days; a slower individualized taper may be needed with longer exposure or a higher dose. If clonidine and a beta blocker are both to be discontinued, the label recommends withdrawing the beta blocker several days before the gradual clonidine taper, under supervision. Consider the beta blocker’s cardiac indication before planning withdrawal. Ensure access to medication and provide clear missed-dose advice. A later transition to a more sustainable long-acting regimen may reduce recurrence, but it should be arranged without creating another abrupt interruption.

Mineralocorticoid excess from primary aldosteronism: Primary aldosteronism is an important cause of sustained or resistant hypertension, often with suppressed renin and sometimes hypokalemia. It does not explain the specific acute withdrawal-related tachyadrenergic pattern as well.

Autonomous catecholamine secretion from a pheochromocytoma: A catecholamine-secreting tumor can produce a similar adrenergic syndrome and merits testing in an appropriate recurrent phenotype. The abrupt onset after interruption of a known sympatholytic is a more direct explanation here.

Thyroid-hormone excess causing increased adrenergic responsiveness: Thyrotoxicosis can cause tremor, sweating and tachycardia, generally with other clinical and biochemical evidence. The medication interruption and short time course favor a withdrawal syndrome rather than newly established thyroid disease.

questions.question: A patient with confirmed resistant hypertension, suitable renal anatomy and eGFR 68 mL/min/1.73 m² asks about catheter-based renal denervation after medication intolerance. Which statement best reflects current evidence?
options: Its main established advantage is protection against kidney failure in advanced CKD
It lowers BP chiefly in untreated patients, with little supporting evidence during drug therapy
Its cardiovascular-event benefit is established to the same degree as its BP-lowering effect
It is a selected adjunct that can lower BP, while direct cardiovascular-event benefit remains unproven
questions.explanation:
Renal Denervation: BP Efficacy and Outcome Uncertainty

Correct answer: It is a selected adjunct that can lower BP, while direct cardiovascular-event benefit remains unproven

Mechanism and Evidence

**Renal denervation disrupts sympathetic signaling around the renal arteries using an approved catheter technology, such as radiofrequency or ultrasound.** Modern sham-controlled trials support modest average BP lowering, with variable individual response.

Evidence exists in selected medicated and unmedicated populations. Trial averages should not be presented as a guaranteed response for a particular patient.

The established evidence concerns pressure reduction. Direct prevention of stroke, myocardial infarction, cardiovascular death or kidney failure has not been established to the same degree; extrapolation from BP lowering should be described as an expectation rather than a proven procedural outcome.

Patient Selection and Follow-Up

**Use shared decision-making within an experienced specialist service after confirming the pressure phenotype and reviewing drug treatment.** Evaluate adherence, out-of-office measurements, secondary causes, renal function and anatomical eligibility.

Discuss alternative drug strategies, expected benefit, procedural risks, uncertainty and the likely need for ongoing medication and follow-up. Drug intolerance can enter the decision, but does not make the procedure mandatory.

Eligibility boundaries depend on the guideline, device and evidence population. Do not assume that a reassuring average safety signal establishes suitability in advanced CKD, major renal-artery disease or a secondary endocrine cause of hypertension. Continue monitoring pressure and renal status after treatment and adjust medicines according to the observed response. Denervation does not replace lifestyle treatment or remove the need to detect pseudoresistance. This question separates a supported selected adjunct from a universal cure or an unproven event-prevention claim, which is essential when translating a BP endpoint into clinical counseling.

ACC 2026 Selection

**The ACC 2026 pathway considers renal denervation in carefully selected patients with office systolic BP ==140–180 mmHg==, diastolic BP at least ==90 mmHg== and eGFR at least ==40 mL/min/1.73 m²==.** Resistant hypertension despite optimized therapy or intolerance of additional medicines can support specialist assessment.

Exclude unsuitable anatomy and conditions such as significant renal-artery stenosis, renal FMD, renal-artery aneurysm or stent, pregnancy, neurogenic orthostatic hypotension and relevant renal or secreting adrenal tumors. Device-specific requirements still apply.

Discuss access-site and renal-artery complications, variable BP response and the likelihood of continued medication. Evidence for hard cardiovascular outcomes remains limited; do not promise cure or medication withdrawal.

Its main established advantage is protection against kidney failure in advanced CKD: The intervention is a BP-lowering adjunct, not an established kidney-failure prevention treatment. Advanced CKD and complex renal anatomy also limit the applicability of much of the trial evidence.

It lowers BP chiefly in untreated patients, with little supporting evidence during drug therapy: Modern sham-controlled studies include both off-medication and on-medication settings. A selected patient already taking antihypertensives is not excluded from potential benefit simply because treatment is ongoing.

Its cardiovascular-event benefit is established to the same degree as its BP-lowering effect: BP reduction is an important intermediate endpoint, but expected risk reduction cannot be substituted for a completed event-driven demonstration of benefit from the procedure itself.

questions.explanationHtml:
Renal Denervation: BP Efficacy and Outcome Uncertainty

Correct answer: D — It is a selected adjunct that can lower BP, while direct cardiovascular-event benefit remains unproven

Mechanism and Evidence

  • Renal denervation disrupts sympathetic signaling around the renal arteries using an approved catheter technology, such as radiofrequency or ultrasound. Modern sham-controlled trials support modest average BP lowering, with variable individual response.
    • Evidence exists in selected medicated and unmedicated populations. Trial averages should not be presented as a guaranteed response for a particular patient.
    • The established evidence concerns pressure reduction. Direct prevention of stroke, myocardial infarction, cardiovascular death or kidney failure has not been established to the same degree; extrapolation from BP lowering should be described as an expectation rather than a proven procedural outcome.

Patient Selection and Follow-Up

  • Use shared decision-making within an experienced specialist service after confirming the pressure phenotype and reviewing drug treatment. Evaluate adherence, out-of-office measurements, secondary causes, renal function and anatomical eligibility.
    • Discuss alternative drug strategies, expected benefit, procedural risks, uncertainty and the likely need for ongoing medication and follow-up. Drug intolerance can enter the decision, but does not make the procedure mandatory.
    • Eligibility boundaries depend on the guideline, device and evidence population. Do not assume that a reassuring average safety signal establishes suitability in advanced CKD, major renal-artery disease or a secondary endocrine cause of hypertension. Continue monitoring pressure and renal status after treatment and adjust medicines according to the observed response. Denervation does not replace lifestyle treatment or remove the need to detect pseudoresistance. This question separates a supported selected adjunct from a universal cure or an unproven event-prevention claim, which is essential when translating a BP endpoint into clinical counseling.

ACC 2026 Selection

  • The ACC 2026 pathway considers renal denervation in carefully selected patients with office systolic BP 140–180 mmHg, diastolic BP at least 90 mmHg and eGFR at least 40 mL/min/1.73 m². Resistant hypertension despite optimized therapy or intolerance of additional medicines can support specialist assessment.
    • Exclude unsuitable anatomy and conditions such as significant renal-artery stenosis, renal FMD, renal-artery aneurysm or stent, pregnancy, neurogenic orthostatic hypotension and relevant renal or secreting adrenal tumors. Device-specific requirements still apply.
    • Discuss access-site and renal-artery complications, variable BP response and the likelihood of continued medication. Evidence for hard cardiovascular outcomes remains limited; do not promise cure or medication withdrawal.

Other Options

  • A — Its main established advantage is protection against kidney failure in advanced CKD: The intervention is a BP-lowering adjunct, not an established kidney-failure prevention treatment. Advanced CKD and complex renal anatomy also limit the applicability of much of the trial evidence.
  • B — It lowers BP chiefly in untreated patients, with little supporting evidence during drug therapy: Modern sham-controlled studies include both off-medication and on-medication settings. A selected patient already taking antihypertensives is not excluded from potential benefit simply because treatment is ongoing.
  • C — Its cardiovascular-event benefit is established to the same degree as its BP-lowering effect: BP reduction is an important intermediate endpoint, but expected risk reduction cannot be substituted for a completed event-driven demonstration of benefit from the procedure itself.

questions.question: Which statement best represents the Endocrine Society 2025 PA screening recommendation, including for adults with controlled hypertension and normal potassium?
options: Reserve screening for failure of three optimally dosed antihypertensives
Reserve screening for hypertension accompanied by spontaneous hypokalemia
Consider aldosterone and renin screening in all hypertensive adults, with resource-dependent implementation
Screen with adrenal CT when potassium is normal and biochemical tests are less informative
questions.explanation:
Primary Aldosteronism: Broader Screening in 2025

Correct answer: Consider aldosterone and renin screening in all hypertensive adults, with resource-dependent implementation

Screening Recommendation

**The Endocrine Society 2025 guidance conditionally suggests PA screening across the hypertensive population.** Feasibility, resources and local expertise affect implementation; this should not be presented as an unconditional mandate for every setting.

Normal potassium does not exclude PA. Renal potassium wasting depends on the degree of mineralocorticoid action and other factors, so overt hypokalemia represents only part of the disease spectrum.

When testing capacity is limited, resistant hypertension, spontaneous or diuretic-associated hypokalemia and other strong clinical clues remain important priorities. An apparently mild BP phenotype can still conceal a specifically treatable cause.

Initial Evaluation

**Measure aldosterone and renin, and interpret their relationship in the clinical and assay context.** Check potassium because hypokalemia can suppress aldosterone and create a misleadingly reassuring result.

Obtain samples under standardized conditions, generally in the morning with the patient seated, without recent dietary sodium restriction. Review medicines that alter renin or aldosterone and plan changes only when clinically safe.

An elevated ratio is a screening clue, not a diagnosis based on arithmetic alone: very low renin can generate a high ratio even when aldosterone is not convincingly elevated. Conversely, a negative test during hypokalemia may need repetition after correction. A positive biochemical assessment leads to an individualized pathway for suppression testing, targeted medical treatment or surgical evaluation. CT cannot replace this physiological assessment because incidental nodules are common and bilateral functional disease may have unremarkable anatomy. Detecting PA matters because treatment can address aldosterone-mediated risk as well as the pressure number.

Reserve screening for failure of three optimally dosed antihypertensives: Resistant hypertension remains a high-priority reason to test. It is not a prerequisite under the broader 2025 recommendation, so good control on one drug does not automatically exclude screening.

Reserve screening for hypertension accompanied by spontaneous hypokalemia: Hypokalemia identifies a particularly important phenotype, but many patients with primary aldosteronism are normokalemic. Restricting testing to this feature would miss cases and is narrower than the current conditional recommendation.

Screen with adrenal CT when potassium is normal and biochemical tests are less informative: CT is useful for adrenal anatomy after appropriate endocrine assessment, especially when surgery is considered. Normal potassium does not make aldosterone and renin uninformative, and an adrenal nodule does not establish functional aldosterone excess.

questions.question: During PA screening, an adult taking metoprolol has potassium 3.0 mmol/L, immunoassay aldosterone 8 ng/dL and PRA 0.1 ng/mL/h. The ARR is 80. What is the best interpretation?
options: Proceed directly to saline suppression using the current potassium and medications
The ratio establishes primary aldosteronism
Aldosterone below 10 ng/dL excludes PA despite the elevated ratio
The result is confounded; correct potassium and repeat with a safe medication strategy
questions.explanation:
Aldosterone–Renin Ratio: Potassium and Medication Effects

Correct answer: The result is confounded; correct potassium and repeat with a safe medication strategy

Biochemical Interpretation

**Interpret aldosterone, renin and the ratio together.** Metoprolol can suppress renin and inflate the ratio; hypokalemia can suppress aldosterone and obscure genuine autonomous secretion.

For commonly used immunoassays, the 2025 guidance gives a typical positive-screen framework of suppressed renin, aldosterone at least ==10 ng/dL== and an ARR above 20 when PRA is expressed in ng/mL/h. Local assay cutoffs and pretest probability still govern interpretation.

LC-MS/MS uses a lower aldosterone boundary, typically ==7.5 ng/dL==, and different ratio calibration. A ratio calculated using direct renin concentration cannot be interpreted with a PRA-based numerical cutoff.

Repeat Testing

**Correct potassium and arrange a clinically safe repeat assessment.** A blanket instruction to stop all antihypertensives is inappropriate in a patient with significant pressure or cardiac risk.

If safe and needed for clarification, beta blockers or central alpha-2 agonists may be withdrawn for about two weeks. MRAs, ENaC blockers and other diuretics generally require a longer, approximately four-week interval; ACE inhibitors and ARBs can also interfere and may require about two weeks.

Minimal-withdrawal or no-withdrawal strategies are possible when necessary, provided the result is interpreted accordingly. Use an alternative regimen selected for the patient rather than creating uncontrolled hypertension to obtain a laboratory sample. In a convincing high-aldosterone phenotype, the presence of beta blockade does not automatically invalidate every positive result. Here the combination of a borderline-low aldosterone, hypokalemia and a renin-lowering drug makes reassessment the defensible choice. Imaging, suppression testing and eventual lateralization answer different questions and should not be inferred from the ratio alone.

Measurement framework | Typical screening guidance; local assay validation required

Low renin for typical screening framework | PRA ==≤1 ng/mL/h== or direct renin ==≤8.2 mU/L==

Immunoassay aldosterone | ==≥10 ng/dL== with suppressed renin

LC-MS/MS aldosterone | ==≥7.5 ng/dL== with suppressed renin

Immunoassay aldosterone [ng/dL]/PRA [ng/mL/h] | >20 with an appropriate aldosterone concentration

Interpretation prerequisite | Review potassium, sodium intake, medications and assay units

Proceed directly to saline suppression using the current potassium and medications: Suppression testing can clarify selected intermediate-probability cases, especially when surgery is being pursued. Correcting the screening confounders first is more appropriate than carrying an uninterpretable baseline directly into a downstream test.

The ratio establishes primary aldosteronism: A high ratio can result from drug-induced renin suppression. Aldosterone is not clearly elevated by the stated immunoassay threshold, while hypokalemia can lower the measured concentration. The present result therefore needs reassessment rather than a definitive PA label.

Aldosterone below 10 ng/dL excludes PA despite the elevated ratio: Aldosterone below a usual cutoff would be reassuring only in an appropriately interpretable setting. Hypokalemia can lower aldosterone, so a single low value here cannot reliably exclude PA.

questions.explanation:
Overt Primary Aldosteronism and Suppression-Test Exceptions

Correct answer: Proceed to the PA-specific localization pathway without routine aldosterone-suppression testing

Biochemical Criteria

**The 2025 pathway does not require a suppression test for every positive screen.** Hypertension with hypokalemia or resistance plus overt renin-independent aldosterone secretion can justify moving directly to PA-specific evaluation.

The guidance describes PRA below ==0.2 ng/mL/h== or direct renin below ==2 mU/L== together with aldosterone above ==20 ng/dL== by immunoassay, or above ==15 ng/dL== by LC-MS/MS, in the relevant phenotype. This patient meets the immunoassay pattern after important confounders have been addressed.

The rationale includes the possibility of a false-negative suppression result in an otherwise compelling case. This is a selected exception, not permission to diagnose PA from every mildly elevated ratio.

Localization and Treatment Planning

**Omitting suppression does not prove unilateral disease.** A patient seeking surgery still needs appropriate adrenal anatomy and usually AVS to establish functional lateralization.

Adrenal CT evaluates structural lesions and possible malignancy. AVS distinguishes lateralizing secretion from bilateral disease when the patient is an appropriate surgical candidate; a visible nodule is not equivalent to an aldosterone-producing source.

For an intermediate-probability result, suppression testing can still be useful after shared decision-making, particularly when it will determine pursuit of surgery. Choose the protocol according to comorbidity, safety and local expertise; sodium-loading procedures can be unsuitable in important volume-sensitive disease. If a patient declines or cannot undergo a surgical pathway, targeted MRA treatment can be appropriate without making every confirmatory procedure a prerequisite. Correct potassium and control pressure throughout the investigation. The critical distinctions are biochemical certainty, functional laterality and willingness or fitness for surgery; each changes the appropriate next step.

Require saline suppression before any PA-specific evaluation: Saline suppression can help selected intermediate-probability cases. In the overt renin-independent phenotype described, the guideline allows its omission and cautions about false-negative suppression results.

Require oral sodium-loading confirmation before adrenal imaging or treatment: Oral sodium loading is another suppression approach for an appropriate selected patient. It is not a mandatory gateway when the supplied clinical and biochemical phenotype already meets the overt-disease exception.

Require fludrocortisone suppression before discussing lateralization: Fludrocortisone suppression can be used in experienced centers with careful potassium and volume monitoring. Its complexity does not make it a required test in every positive PA assessment.

questions.question: A 56-year-old with established PA wants definitive surgery if appropriate. CT shows a 1.6-cm left adrenal adenoma and a normal-appearing right adrenal. What is the best test to guide the side of surgery?
options: Repeat CT with washout calculations to identify the secreting side
Adrenal venous sampling in an experienced center
Repeat the peripheral ARR to determine whether the left gland is dominant

questions.explanation:
Adrenal CT and Functional Lateralization in PA

Correct answer: Adrenal venous sampling in an experienced center

Anatomy Versus Function

**CT and AVS answer complementary questions.** CT defines adrenal anatomy and identifies lesions requiring structural evaluation; AVS measures side-specific hormone secretion.

A small aldosterone-producing lesion may not be visible, a visible lesion may be nonfunctioning, and both glands may contribute. Normal right-sided anatomy therefore does not prove absence of right-sided aldosterone production.

AVS requires successful selective sampling and protocol-specific interpretation, generally accounting for dilution using cortisol or another validated approach. Technical success and local expertise matter before assigning a lateralization result.

Surgical Eligibility and Associated Hormone Secretion

questions.question: A patient with bilateral PA takes spironolactone 25 mg daily. BP remains 150/92 mmHg and renin remains suppressed. Potassium is 3.8 mmol/L, eGFR 82 mL/min/1.73 m² and there are no limiting adverse effects. Which adjustment best follows the Endocrine Society 2025 treatment approach?
options: Add doxazosin 1 mg at night
Add amlodipine 5 mg daily
Replace spironolactone with amiloride 5 mg daily
Increase spironolactone to 50 mg daily
questions.explanation:
Medical Treatment of Bilateral Primary Aldosteronism

Correct answer: Increase spironolactone to 50 mg daily

Disease-Specific Treatment

**Bilateral PA is generally managed medically with mineralocorticoid receptor blockade.** In lateralizing disease, a suitable patient who wants surgery may instead receive unilateral adrenalectomy after appropriate evaluation.

A common low spironolactone starting dose is ==12.5–25 mg== daily. The current 25-mg dose can be increased, for example to ==50 mg== daily, when laboratory findings, pressure and tolerance permit; some PA patients need further specialist-guided titration.

The 2025 recommendation specifically supports increasing aldosterone-directed treatment when BP remains uncontrolled and renin is still suppressed. It does not specify one universal numerical renin target.

Monitoring and Limitations

**Follow potassium, kidney function and symptoms during titration.** Potassium supplements and other antihypertensives may need adjustment as aldosterone action is blocked and pressure falls.

Check early laboratory responses according to renal and potassium risk. A modest fall in filtration can reflect correction of aldosterone-associated hyperfiltration, but a large deterioration, symptomatic hypotension or hyperkalemia requires reassessment.

Spironolactone can cause breast tenderness, gynecomastia or menstrual effects; a more selective MRA may be appropriate if these become limiting. Reducing sodium intake supports the treatment response. When pressure is already controlled, the clinical benefit of escalating solely to raise renin remains uncertain, so that different scenario should not be confused with this uncontrolled patient. An unchanged suppressed renin value also requires interpretation with concomitant medicines and the overall response. The objective is adequate disease-specific treatment with safe pressure and electrolyte control, not pursuit of an isolated biomarker regardless of adverse effects.

Add doxazosin 1 mg at night: An alpha blocker can lower pressure, including during selected endocrine testing strategies. It does not address insufficient aldosterone blockade as directly as titrating a tolerated MRA in this phenotype.

Add amlodipine 5 mg daily: A CCB can be a useful additional BP drug. Here persistent hypertension with suppressed renin and well-tolerated low-dose MRA treatment supports optimizing aldosterone-directed therapy first.

Replace spironolactone with amiloride 5 mg daily: An ENaC blocker can be an alternative when MRAs cannot be used or tolerated. It is less directly aligned with the recommended PA-specific strategy when an MRA is safe and has not yet been adequately titrated.

Endocrine Society primary aldosteronism guideline, 2025 — https://www.endocrine.org/clinical-practice-guidelines/primary-aldosteronism-2

AHA/ACC high blood pressure guideline, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001356

questions.question: In a patient being evaluated for renovascular hypertension, a technically adequate renal duplex shows a focal renal-artery peak systolic velocity of 240 cm/s and a renal–aortic velocity ratio of 4.0. Which interpretation best follows the ESC 2024 vascular guideline?
options: The findings support significant renal-artery narrowing but do not alone establish benefit from revascularization
The findings support severe renal parenchymal disease without renal-artery narrowing
The findings support a critical lesion for which catheter angiography should be the next test
The findings support an arteriovenous shunt as the primary explanation for the raised ratio
questions.explanation:
Renal-Artery Duplex: Anatomy, Hemodynamics and Causality

Correct answer: The findings support significant renal-artery narrowing but do not alone establish benefit from revascularization

Duplex Principle and Thresholds

**Duplex combines anatomical imaging with flow velocity and waveform assessment.** A focal accelerated jet and a raised renal–aortic velocity ratio support stenosis when the examination is technically reliable.

ESC 2024 reports renal-artery peak systolic velocity above ==200 cm/s== for greater than ==50%== stenosis and a renal–aortic ratio above 3.5 for at least ==60%== stenosis. The supplied values exceed both criteria; these are named guideline criteria rather than a universal laboratory calibration.

The ratio divides renal-artery by aortic peak systolic velocity. Aortic flow abnormalities, Doppler angle, vessel tortuosity, accessory arteries, obesity and bowel gas can limit interpretation. Post-stenotic turbulence and tardus–parvus intrarenal waveforms may provide supporting information.

Competing Tests and Management Implications

**An anatomical or velocity threshold does not prove that the stenosis causes the patient’s hypertension.** Review onset, treatment resistance, kidney function, renal size and recurrent circulatory episodes.

CTA defines vascular anatomy well but involves iodinated contrast and radiation. MRA offers another anatomical route with modality- and contrast-specific limitations. Invasive angiography is mainly reserved for unresolved diagnostic questions or planned intervention and can measure translesional gradients.

Continue BP and vascular-risk treatment when stable atherosclerotic stenosis is managed medically. Recurrent flash pulmonary edema, progressive ischemic kidney dysfunction or selected refractory cases may justify specialist revascularization review. Assess kidney viability and distinguish atherosclerotic ostial disease from FMD, for which balloon angioplasty rather than routine primary stenting is the usual intervention when indicated. An equivocal or technically inadequate study requires another assessment rather than forced grading from an unreliable velocity.

The findings support severe renal parenchymal disease without renal-artery narrowing: Parenchymal disease can produce hypertension and abnormal intrarenal indices, but focal main-artery velocity acceleration with a raised renal–aortic ratio supports an arterial stenotic lesion. Parenchymal assessment remains complementary rather than the explanation of these specific measurements.

The findings support a critical lesion for which catheter angiography should be the next test: Catheter angiography is appropriate when intervention is being considered or noninvasive testing leaves an important unresolved question. These velocities support narrowing but do not establish a critical lesion or a clinical indication for an invasive next step; stable atherosclerotic disease commonly remains on medical care.

The findings support an arteriovenous shunt as the primary explanation for the raised ratio: An arteriovenous communication can increase flow but requires its own Doppler features, including an appropriate low-resistance arterial and arterialized venous pattern. Focal stenotic acceleration and the supplied ratio are interpreted in a renal-artery stenosis pathway rather than diagnosing a shunt from velocity alone.

ESC peripheral arterial and aortic diseases guideline, 2024 — https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/article/45/36/3538/7738955

AIUM native renal vessel duplex practice parameter, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1002/jum.16353
