questions.question: Which renal-artery stenosis phenotype most strongly supports specialist consideration of revascularization?
options: Unilateral 70% atherosclerotic stenosis with stable renal function and controlled BP
Severe bilateral renal-artery disease with recurrent flash pulmonary edema despite medical care
Bilateral moderate stenoses with stable renal function and no circulatory episodes
An incidental severe lesion supplying a small atrophic kidney with controlled BP
questions.explanation:
Renal-Artery Stenosis: Selecting Revascularization Review

Correct answer: Severe bilateral renal-artery disease with recurrent flash pulmonary edema despite medical care

Trial Interpretation

**CORAL did not establish a routine clinical-event benefit from adding renal-artery stenting to comprehensive medical care in the studied atherosclerotic population.** This argues against treating a percentage stenosis alone.

Medical care includes pressure control, atherosclerotic risk reduction and monitoring of kidney function. Renin–angiotensin blockade can be useful but requires careful renal and potassium surveillance, especially when bilateral hemodynamically important disease is suspected.

A trial’s average result should not be converted into a prohibition on investigating every high-risk presentation. Some unstable syndromes were poorly represented in routine-intervention trials.

High-Risk Clinical Syndromes

**Recurrent flash pulmonary edema associated with severe renovascular disease is a recognized reason for selective multidisciplinary review.** Other concerning patterns can include rapidly worsening kidney function or difficult pressure control when a hemodynamically important lesion plausibly contributes.

Assess whether the kidney is viable and the syndrome is attributable to renovascular disease. Before intervention, consensus criteria for lesion significance include more than ==70%== luminal narrowing, a mean translesional gradient above ==10 mmHg== or renal fractional flow reserve below 0.8; these findings still require a compatible clinical indication.

Benefits reported in selected pulmonary-edema cohorts are largely observational, so do not present intervention as a guaranteed mortality or kidney-failure benefit. Continue medical stabilization and risk-factor treatment while specialist assessment proceeds. The choice of angioplasty, stenting or another approach depends on the lesion; atherosclerotic ostial disease and renal FMD do not share an identical procedural strategy. Follow BP, renal function and recurrence after any intervention because revascularization does not erase coexisting vascular disease or primary hypertension.

Unilateral 70% atherosclerotic stenosis with stable renal function and controlled BP: Anatomic narrowing alone does not establish benefit from intervention. Stable kidney function and effective medical control favor continued vascular-risk and BP management with surveillance.

Bilateral moderate stenoses with stable renal function and no circulatory episodes: Moderate anatomical lesions do not necessarily produce important renal ischemia. Without an attributable high-risk syndrome, routine stenting is not supported simply because both arteries appear abnormal.

An incidental severe lesion supplying a small atrophic kidney with controlled BP: A severe image finding can draw attention, but an atrophic kidney may have limited recoverable function. Assess viability and the overall syndrome rather than assuming that opening every severe lesion improves outcomes.

CORAL: renal-artery stenting and medical therapy — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24245566/

questions.question: A 31-year-old woman has confirmed difficult-to-control hypertension and hemodynamically important multifocal renal FMD. A specialist team has selected revascularization. Which initial procedural strategy is generally preferred?
options: Primary covered-stent placement across the affected segment
Primary bare-metal stenting of the affected renal segment
Balloon angioplasty without routine stent placement
Open aortorenal bypass as the first procedure
questions.explanation:
Renal Fibromuscular Dysplasia: Angioplasty Strategy

Correct answer: Balloon angioplasty without routine stent placement

Disease Pattern and Evaluation

**Renal FMD is a nonatherosclerotic arterial disorder that can cause renovascular hypertension, often in younger adults.** Multifocal disease commonly produces alternating narrowing and dilatation in mid-to-distal arterial segments.

That distribution differs from the usual ostial or proximal atherosclerotic lesion. Clinical age and a beaded appearance support the diagnosis, but the decision to intervene also requires assessment of lesion significance and the pressure phenotype.

A visible lesion need not be the only contributor to hypertension. Confirm adherence and out-of-office pressure, review renal function and consider the likelihood of a meaningful treatment response before selecting revascularization.

Treatment and Follow-Up

**When intervention is indicated, balloon angioplasty without routine stenting is the usual FMD strategy.** Stent placement is reserved for specific circumstances such as a flow-limiting dissection or another complication rather than used automatically.

Young age, a shorter hypertension history and a favorable lesion can improve the prospect of response, but cure is not assured. Some patients still need antihypertensive treatment after technically successful angioplasty.

Monitor renal function, access-site complications, BP and possible restenosis. FMD can involve more than one vascular territory; assess associated aneurysm or dissection risk using an appropriate vascular evaluation rather than treating the kidney image as an isolated finding. Medical BP treatment remains appropriate when the lesion is not a good procedural target or expected benefit is low. Atherosclerotic-stenting trial results cannot be transferred uncritically to this distinct disease. Conversely, a successful FMD procedure is not evidence that an older patient with an incidental atherosclerotic lesion should undergo routine intervention.

Primary covered-stent placement across the affected segment: A covered stent can be useful for selected aneurysms, rupture or other vascular complications. It is not the default treatment of an uncomplicated stenotic FMD segment.

Primary bare-metal stenting of the affected renal segment: Stenting is commonly used for selected atherosclerotic renal lesions and may be needed as a bailout for a procedural complication. Routine primary stenting is not the preferred FMD strategy.

Open aortorenal bypass as the first procedure: Surgery retains a role for complex anatomy, associated aneurysm or failed endovascular treatment. When a suitable FMD lesion can be treated percutaneously, balloon angioplasty is generally the initial approach.

questions.explanationHtml:
Renal Fibromuscular Dysplasia: Angioplasty Strategy

Correct answer: C — Balloon angioplasty without routine stent placement

Disease Pattern and Evaluation

  • Renal FMD is a nonatherosclerotic arterial disorder that can cause renovascular hypertension, often in younger adults. Multifocal disease commonly produces alternating narrowing and dilatation in mid-to-distal arterial segments.
    • That distribution differs from the usual ostial or proximal atherosclerotic lesion. Clinical age and a beaded appearance support the diagnosis, but the decision to intervene also requires assessment of lesion significance and the pressure phenotype.
    • A visible lesion need not be the only contributor to hypertension. Confirm adherence and out-of-office pressure, review renal function and consider the likelihood of a meaningful treatment response before selecting revascularization.

Treatment and Follow-Up

  • When intervention is indicated, balloon angioplasty without routine stenting is the usual FMD strategy. Stent placement is reserved for specific circumstances such as a flow-limiting dissection or another complication rather than used automatically.
    • Young age, a shorter hypertension history and a favorable lesion can improve the prospect of response, but cure is not assured. Some patients still need antihypertensive treatment after technically successful angioplasty.
    • Monitor renal function, access-site complications, BP and possible restenosis. FMD can involve more than one vascular territory; assess associated aneurysm or dissection risk using an appropriate vascular evaluation rather than treating the kidney image as an isolated finding. Medical BP treatment remains appropriate when the lesion is not a good procedural target or expected benefit is low. Atherosclerotic-stenting trial results cannot be transferred uncritically to this distinct disease. Conversely, a successful FMD procedure is not evidence that an older patient with an incidental atherosclerotic lesion should undergo routine intervention.

Other Options

  • A — Primary covered-stent placement across the affected segment: A covered stent can be useful for selected aneurysms, rupture or other vascular complications. It is not the default treatment of an uncomplicated stenotic FMD segment.
  • B — Primary bare-metal stenting of the affected renal segment: Stenting is commonly used for selected atherosclerotic renal lesions and may be needed as a bailout for a procedural complication. Routine primary stenting is not the preferred FMD strategy.
  • D — Open aortorenal bypass as the first procedure: Surgery retains a role for complex anatomy, associated aneurysm or failed endovascular treatment. When a suitable FMD lesion can be treated percutaneously, balloon angioplasty is generally the initial approach.

  • AHA renovascular revascularization scientific statement, 2022
  • ESC elevated blood pressure and hypertension guideline, 2024

questions.question: An obese adult with resistant hypertension, loud snoring, witnessed apneas and daytime sleepiness has a technically adequate but negative home sleep-apnea test. Clinical suspicion remains high. Which investigation is most appropriate next?
options: Attended overnight polysomnography
Repeat home sleep-apnea testing
Overnight pulse oximetry alone
Multiple sleep latency testing
questions.explanation:
Suspected OSA After a Negative Home Sleep Test

Correct answer: Attended overnight polysomnography

Diagnostic Testing

**A negative home test does not reliably exclude OSA when the clinical probability remains high.** Home systems may underestimate event frequency because recording time can exceed actual sleep time and because their signals and scoring differ from laboratory polysomnography.

Polysomnography records sleep and respiratory physiology more comprehensively. It is also preferred from the outset in important cardiorespiratory disease, suspected hypoventilation, certain neuromuscular disorders, chronic opioid use, previous stroke or severe insomnia.

A screening questionnaire or a characteristic symptom cluster estimates risk but does not independently establish the diagnosis. Confirming OSA also allows treatment planning based on severity, symptoms and comorbidity.

Hypertension and Treatment

**Intermittent hypoxemia, arousals and sympathetic activation can contribute to resistant and nocturnal hypertension.** Assess the sleep phenotype without assuming that it is the only cause of poor BP control.

CPAP can improve OSA-related symptoms and can produce a generally modest, adherence-dependent BP improvement. It should complement weight management, pressure medication and review of other contributors rather than be presented as a guaranteed replacement for antihypertensives.

Follow device use, residual events, symptoms and home or ambulatory pressure after treatment. Persistent daytime sleepiness despite adequate OSA treatment may warrant evaluation for other causes. Avoid converting a favorable sleep or BP response into an unsupported claim that every treated patient has a proven reduction in cardiovascular events. The immediate decision here is diagnostic: use the more definitive overnight assessment rather than dismissing a high-probability clinical presentation because one limited home study was negative.

Repeat home sleep-apnea testing: Home testing is useful in selected uncomplicated adults at increased risk. AASM guidance recommends polysomnography after a single negative, inconclusive or technically inadequate home test when OSA remains suspected, rather than using repeated home testing as the default response.

Overnight pulse oximetry alone: Oximetry can reveal desaturation and assist selected assessments, but it lacks the full respiratory and sleep information needed to resolve a negative home study with persistent clinical suspicion. A normal oximetry result also does not exclude OSA.

Multiple sleep latency testing: This test evaluates selected central hypersomnolence disorders after appropriate overnight assessment. It does not replace the respiratory sleep study required to investigate suspected obstructive events in this setting.

HIPARCO randomized CPAP trial in resistant hypertension — https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/1788459

questions.question: A patient with a functional adrenal pheochromocytoma is being prepared for elective surgery. BP is 172/100 mmHg and sinus rate 116/min. Which preparation strategy is most appropriate?
options: Start phenoxybenzamine and propranolol together with the first doses
Start a beta blocker first, adding an alpha blocker after the rate is controlled
Use labetalol alone as the initial complete adrenergic-blocking regimen
Establish adequate alpha blockade, then add a beta blocker if tachycardia persists
questions.explanation:
Pheochromocytoma: Alpha and Beta Blockade Sequencing

Correct answer: Establish adequate alpha blockade, then add a beta blocker if tachycardia persists

Pathophysiology and Treatment Sequence

**Catecholamine-related vasoconstriction must be addressed before introducing beta blockade for tachycardia.** The sequence protects against an abrupt increase in alpha-mediated vascular resistance.

Functional PPGL generally requires a specialist preoperative preparation plan. Alpha blockade is usually titrated over about 7–14 days, with the exact period guided by pressure, postural tolerance, heart rate and comorbidity.

Phenoxybenzamine or a selective alpha-1 blocker such as doxazosin can be used. A common doxazosin starting dose is ==1–2 mg== daily, with cautious escalation according to the monitored response; regimens are individualized rather than based on a single fixed dose for all patients.

Volume Status and Monitoring

**Assess seated and standing pressure, symptoms and volume status throughout preparation.** Catecholamine excess can contract the effective circulating volume, and appropriate salt and fluid replacement after blockade can reduce perioperative instability.

Volume expansion requires particular care in heart failure or kidney disease. Add a suitable beta blocker only after adequate alpha blockade if tachycardia remains a treatment problem; do not chase the rate while ignoring vascular resistance.

Anesthesia, surgery and endocrine teams should coordinate medication and intraoperative planning. Severe acute catecholamine crises require a monitored emergency approach rather than merely following an outpatient titration schedule. Calcium-channel blockers or metyrosine can be useful in selected situations, but do not make mixed alpha/beta blockade interchangeable with the usual preparation sequence. After surgery, monitor hypotension and glucose as well as the possibility of persistent disease. The presence of tachycardia therefore changes the eventual combination, while the alpha-first requirement determines its order.

Start phenoxybenzamine and propranolol together with the first doses: The two agents may both be used during preparation, but alpha blockade needs to be established before beta blockade is added. Starting both simultaneously does not demonstrate that protective sequence.

Start a beta blocker first, adding an alpha blocker after the rate is controlled: Rate control can be appropriate after alpha blockade. Starting it first can remove beta-mediated vasodilatation while alpha-mediated vasoconstriction remains active, provoking a dangerous pressure rise.

Use labetalol alone as the initial complete adrenergic-blocking regimen: Labetalol has both actions, but its beta-blocking effect predominates and it is not a reliable substitute for adequate initial alpha blockade in this preparation pathway.

Endocrine Society PPGL guideline, 2014 — https://doi.org/10.1210/jc.2014-1498

Japan Endocrine Society PPGL guideline, 2025 — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12819074/

questions.question: A 19-year-old with familial early-onset hypertension has hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, suppressed renin and low aldosterone. Testing identifies a pathogenic gain-of-function SCNN1B variant. Which drug most directly addresses the mechanism?
options: Eplerenone
Spironolactone
Amiloride
Dexamethasone
questions.explanation:
Liddle Syndrome: ENaC-Directed Treatment

Correct answer: Amiloride

Genetics and Pathophysiology

**Liddle syndrome is an inherited gain-of-function disorder of the epithelial sodium channel.** Increased distal sodium reabsorption expands volume and promotes potassium and hydrogen loss, suppressing renin and aldosterone.

SCNN1B and SCNN1G are characteristic genes. The phenotype can be variably expressed, so lack of hypokalemia in another affected relative does not exclude a pathogenic familial variant.

Low renin alone does not distinguish the syndrome from PA; the low aldosterone and the molecular result identify a different mechanism. Apparent mineralocorticoid excess and liquorice exposure can also produce low-renin, low-aldosterone hypertension and require a different etiological assessment.

Treatment and Monitoring

**Amiloride directly blocks ENaC and is combined with dietary sodium reduction.** A common starting dose is ==5 mg== daily, titrated according to BP, potassium, renal function and the individual response.

Triamterene is another ENaC-blocking option. Monitor potassium and kidney function as treatment corrects potassium wasting; a potassium-sparing drug can still cause hyperkalemia when kidney function changes or interacting medicines are added.

Review potassium supplements and avoid assuming that lifelong hypokalemia makes monitoring unnecessary. Offer appropriate genetic counseling and assessment of at-risk relatives when a pathogenic familial variant is established. Longstanding hypertension can cause cardiac, cerebral and kidney complications even when the patient is young, so durable treatment and follow-up matter. A response to amiloride can support the physiological reasoning, but it should not replace evaluation of other low-renin disorders when the genetic diagnosis is uncertain. The treatment distinction is between blocking an overactive channel and blocking an upstream hormone receptor that is not driving this case.

Condition | Renin / aldosterone pattern | Treatment principle

Primary aldosteronism | Low renin; aldosterone inappropriate or high | MRA or selected unilateral surgery

Liddle syndrome | Both suppressed | ENaC blockade and sodium reduction

Apparent mineralocorticoid excess or liquorice effect | Often both suppressed | Identify cause; reduce mineralocorticoid action

Gordon syndrome | Low-renin hypertension with hyperkalemia/acidosis | Thiazide-sensitive sodium transport phenotype

Eplerenone: Eplerenone is a more selective MRA and can replace spironolactone for selected adverse effects. Its greater receptor specificity does not correct constitutive ENaC overactivity downstream of the mineralocorticoid receptor.

Spironolactone: Spironolactone targets mineralocorticoid receptor activation and is useful in PA and other selected aldosterone-mediated states. The channel abnormality here drives sodium reabsorption despite suppressed aldosterone, so receptor antagonism is not the most direct treatment.

Dexamethasone: Glucocorticoid suppression can be relevant to ACTH-dependent familial hyperaldosteronism after appropriate diagnosis. That is an aldosterone-producing disorder, whereas this patient has a demonstrated sodium-channel mechanism with low aldosterone.

AHA/ACC high blood pressure guideline, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001356

Amiloride prescribing information, DailyMed — https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=2b70cf0c-45be-428f-b396-5001ed4e30fc

questions.question: A 35-year-old with hypertension has progressive proximal weakness, easy bruising and wide violaceous striae. She takes an estrogen-containing oral contraceptive, uses no glucocorticoids and has a regular sleep schedule. Serum cortisol is 4.2 µg/dL after a 1-mg overnight dexamethasone test. Which next step best clarifies endogenous cortisol excess before localization?
options: Perform an 8-mg overnight dexamethasone test
Obtain pituitary contrast MRI
Obtain adrenal CT with washout characterization
Obtain late-night salivary cortisol on two separate nights
questions.explanation:
Hypercortisolism Testing During Oral Estrogen Use

Correct answer: Obtain late-night salivary cortisol on two separate nights

Cortisol Binding and Test Interpretation

**Oral estrogen raises cortisol-binding globulin and can elevate total serum cortisol despite adequate suppression of free cortisol.** The abnormal low-dose result therefore warrants confirmation rather than immediate pituitary or adrenal localization.

The overnight test commonly gives ==1 mg== dexamethasone near 23:00 and measures serum cortisol around 08:00. A result above ==1.8 µg/dL== is an abnormal screen under the usual sensitive cutoff, not proof of a particular tumor.

Late-night saliva assesses free cortisol and loss of the circadian nadir without the same binding-globulin effect. Obtain at least two samples and interpret against the laboratory’s assay-specific range. A regular sleep schedule makes this option suitable; shift work or disrupted sleep can undermine interpretation.

Confirmation and Etiological Evaluation

**Choose complementary biochemical testing and review confounders before assigning a source.** Repeated urinary free cortisol collections are another first-line option, while exogenous glucocorticoid exposure must be sought explicitly.

Review adherence to dexamethasone, interacting drugs that change its clearance, alcohol-related or other non-neoplastic hypercortisolism and conditions affecting cortisol binding. If a serum suppression test is repeated after stopping oral estrogen, arrange suitable contraception and an adequate washout rather than stopping it without a plan.

Concordant positive results on appropriate tests support proceeding to ACTH-guided source evaluation. Discordance, cyclic symptoms or high clinical suspicion despite normal testing merits specialist reassessment. Treat the associated BP, glucose and potassium abnormalities while the investigation proceeds; biochemical clarification and cardiovascular-risk treatment are complementary. The progressive discriminatory physical findings justify assessment, whereas uncomplicated hypertension or obesity alone does not justify indiscriminate cortisol screening.

Perform an 8-mg overnight dexamethasone test: High-dose dexamethasone has sometimes been used as an adjunct in differentiating ACTH-dependent sources, with important limitations. It is not the preferred confirmation test for an oral-estrogen-confounded low-dose screen and does not replace reliable initial biochemical assessment.

Obtain pituitary contrast MRI: Pituitary MRI becomes useful in an appropriate ACTH-dependent localization pathway after endogenous hypercortisolism is established. Incidental pituitary lesions are common enough that imaging before biochemical confirmation can misdirect the diagnosis.

Obtain adrenal CT with washout characterization: Adrenal imaging is used when an adrenal source is supported, typically with confirmed cortisol excess and suppressed ACTH. A single potentially confounded serum suppression result does not establish either cortisol excess or its adrenal origin.

Obtain at least two samples and interpret against the laboratory’s assay-specific range. A regular sleep schedule makes this option suitable; shift work or disrupted sleep can undermine interpretation.

Confirmation and Etiological Evaluation

  • Choose complementary biochemical testing and review confounders before assigning a source. Repeated urinary free cortisol collections are another first-line option, while exogenous glucocorticoid exposure must be sought explicitly.
    • Review adherence to dexamethasone, interacting drugs that change its clearance, alcohol-related or other non-neoplastic hypercortisolism and conditions affecting cortisol binding. If a serum suppression test is repeated after stopping oral estrogen, arrange suitable contraception and an adequate washout rather than stopping it without a plan.
    • Concordant positive results on appropriate tests support proceeding to ACTH-guided source evaluation. Discordance, cyclic symptoms or high clinical suspicion despite normal testing merits specialist reassessment. Treat the associated BP, glucose and potassium abnormalities while the investigation proceeds; biochemical clarification and cardiovascular-risk treatment are complementary. The progressive discriminatory physical findings justify assessment, whereas uncomplicated hypertension or obesity alone does not justify indiscriminate cortisol screening.

Other Options

  • A — Perform an 8-mg overnight dexamethasone test: High-dose dexamethasone has sometimes been used as an adjunct in differentiating ACTH-dependent sources, with important limitations. It is not the preferred confirmation test for an oral-estrogen-confounded low-dose screen and does not replace reliable initial biochemical assessment.
  • B — Obtain pituitary contrast MRI: Pituitary MRI becomes useful in an appropriate ACTH-dependent localization pathway after endogenous hypercortisolism is established. Incidental pituitary lesions are common enough that imaging before biochemical confirmation can misdirect the diagnosis.
  • C — Obtain adrenal CT with washout characterization: Adrenal imaging is used when an adrenal source is supported, typically with confirmed cortisol excess and suppressed ACTH. A single potentially confounded serum suppression result does not establish either cortisol excess or its adrenal origin.

questions.question: A 28-year-old has BP 170/94 mmHg in both arms and systolic pressure 112 mmHg in the legs. Femoral upstrokes are delayed relative to the radial pulses, and there is a systolic murmur over the left interscapular region. Which diagnosis best localizes the cause?
options: Coarctation of the proximal descending thoracic aorta
Renal-artery fibromuscular dysplasia
Takayasu arteritis involving the aortic arch branches
Aortoiliac atherosclerotic occlusive disease
questions.explanation:
Coarctation as a Cause of Young-Onset Hypertension

Correct answer: Coarctation of the proximal descending thoracic aorta

Clinical Localization

**Upper-body hypertension with delayed lower-limb arterial upstrokes suggests an obstruction between the arm and leg circulations.** A posterior thoracic murmur supports coarctation rather than an isolated endocrine or renal-artery cause.

Measure pressure in both arms and a lower extremity using appropriate technique. An arm–leg systolic difference above ==20 mmHg== is an important signal, but a modest measured gradient does not exclude severe disease when collateral flow or reduced ventricular output affects the result.

Assess associated bicuspid aortic valve, ventricular hypertrophy and other congenital findings. Absence of a childhood diagnosis does not exclude presentation in adulthood.

Imaging, Treatment and Follow-Up

**CMR or CT angiography defines the thoracic aorta, narrowing, arch anatomy and collaterals.** Echocardiography assesses associated valve disease, ventricular function and Doppler findings.

Do not equate a Doppler peak instantaneous gradient with an invasive peak-to-peak gradient. Contemporary aortic guidance uses the clinical pressure phenotype, anatomy and appropriate hemodynamic evidence together when deciding intervention.

Significant native or recurrent coarctation with hypertension merits congenital/aortic specialist assessment for stenting or surgery according to anatomy and suitability. Treat pressure medically while planning care, and continue surveillance after repair because residual hypertension, recurrent narrowing and aneurysm can occur. The 2025 ACHD guidance reinforces arm-and-leg BP assessment and individualized long-term imaging. Screening for associated intracranial aneurysms may be considered in selected adult guidance rather than treated as an automatic identical rule across all societies. Repair of the narrowing is not a reason to abandon lifelong cardiovascular follow-up or ignore pressure outside the clinic.

Renal-artery fibromuscular dysplasia: Renal FMD is an important cause of young-onset hypertension and may produce an abdominal bruit. It does not by itself produce a fixed arm–leg pressure difference and radiofemoral delay from an aortic obstruction.

Takayasu arteritis involving the aortic arch branches: Large-vessel vasculitis can cause hypertension and pulse abnormalities. Arch-branch involvement more often produces arm asymmetry or upper-limb pulse deficits; the symmetrical arm pressure and lower-body delay with a posterior thoracic murmur favor coarctation in this stem.

Aortoiliac atherosclerotic occlusive disease: Distal aortic disease can reduce leg pressure and pulses, but usually occurs in a different vascular-risk and symptom context. It does not explain the characteristic posterior thoracic murmur as well as a congenital thoracic narrowing.

ESC elevated blood pressure and hypertension guideline, 2024 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehae178

questions.topic: Hypertensive emergencies and severe asymptomatic pressure
questions.question: Which presentation most clearly establishes a hypertensive emergency?
options: BP 226/130 mmHg with stable creatinine and longstanding ECG LVH
BP 188/114 mmHg with new hypoxemic pulmonary edema
BP 204/118 mmHg with anxiety and a normal neurological examination
BP 194/112 mmHg with chronic retinal arteriovenous nicking
questions.explanation:
Hypertensive Emergency and Acute Organ Injury

Correct answer: BP 188/114 mmHg with new hypoxemic pulmonary edema

Diagnostic Criteria

**A hypertensive emergency is severe BP elevation associated with new or worsening acute target-organ injury.** The supplied pulmonary edema represents acute cardiac injury even though its pressure is lower than that of another option.

Possible syndromes include hypertensive encephalopathy, acute pulmonary edema, acute coronary ischemia, aortic syndromes, acute kidney injury and severe retinal injury. Evaluate the relationship between the pressure and the organ syndrome rather than assigning causality from coexistence alone.

A frequently used severe-pressure boundary is above ==180/120 mmHg==, but a rapid rise or a specific setting can produce an emergency at lower values. Pregnancy has its own severe-range threshold and treatment urgency.

Initial Assessment and Treatment

**Stabilize the affected organ system while determining the appropriate rate of pressure reduction.** Repeat an accurate measurement, assess airway and oxygenation, obtain vascular access and arrange monitored care when indicated.

Direct testing to the presentation: neurological findings may require urgent brain imaging; ischemic symptoms require ECG and troponin assessment; renal evaluation includes creatinine, electrolytes and urinalysis. Examine for aortic and retinal clues rather than ordering the same exhaustive panel for everyone.

Use titratable treatment when an acute syndrome requires it. The target and speed depend on the organ involved: aortic dissection, ischemic stroke, ICH and pregnancy cannot be managed by one generic schedule. Chronic LVH, stable CKD or an isolated high reading still matters, but does not by itself justify rapid intravenous normalization. After stabilization, investigate contributors and establish a sustainable oral regimen with follow-up. The defining distinction is the acute injury, not which patient has the highest recorded number.

BP 226/130 mmHg with stable creatinine and longstanding ECG LVH: Severe pressure and LVH indicate substantial chronic risk, but stable established structural damage is not the acute organ injury that defines an emergency. The patient still needs prompt clinical assessment and a durable treatment plan.

BP 204/118 mmHg with anxiety and a normal neurological examination: Anxiety may contribute to an elevated reading, and symptoms require assessment. Without evidence of acute brain, cardiac, renal or vascular injury, the number alone does not establish a hypertensive emergency.

BP 194/112 mmHg with chronic retinal arteriovenous nicking: Arteriovenous nicking can reflect longstanding hypertensive vascular change. It should not be equated with new hemorrhagic/exudative retinopathy, papilledema or another acute organ-injury syndrome.

AHA/ACC high blood pressure guideline, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001356

questions.topic: Hypertensive emergencies and severe asymptomatic pressure
questions.question: Under AHA/ACC 2025, which reduction sequence applies to a hypertensive emergency without a condition requiring a different target, such as an acute aortic syndrome, stroke or pregnancy?
options: Lower SBP directly to 130–139 mmHg and maintain that range for the first week
Reduce SBP to below 120 mmHg immediately and maintain heart rate at 60–80/min
Allow the pressure to remain unchanged initially and reduce it about 15% over the first day
Reduce SBP by no more than 25% in hour one, then toward below 160/100 over the next 2–6 hours
questions.explanation:
Controlled Initial BP Reduction in a General Hypertensive Emergency

Correct answer: Reduce SBP by no more than 25% in hour one, then toward below 160/100 over the next 2–6 hours

Reduction Sequence

**AHA/ACC 2025 recommends limiting the initial systolic fall to no more than ==25%== during the first hour in the general pathway.** If the patient remains stable, lower toward below ==160/100 mmHg== during the next two to six hours.

Further cautious reduction toward a systolic pressure of ==130–140 mmHg== occurs over roughly twenty-four to forty-eight hours. These stages are a monitored clinical plan, not instructions to force each number despite deteriorating perfusion.

Older teaching often expresses a similar early principle using MAP. Specify the framework and variable being quoted: the 2025 American recommendation is stated in terms of SBP, while syndrome-specific protocols may use other measures.

Autoregulation and Monitoring

**An abrupt excessive fall can reduce cerebral, coronary or renal perfusion.** Chronic hypertension shifts autoregulatory relationships, so an apparently desirable normal pressure may initially be poorly tolerated.

Use repeated clinical and pressure assessment, ideally with appropriate continuous monitoring when an infusion is required. Follow mental state, neurological examination, chest symptoms, urine output and kidney function as relevant.

Identify the acute organ syndrome before applying the general schedule. Dissection needs rapid control of wall stress, ischemic stroke requires attention to reperfusion eligibility and cerebral perfusion, and pregnancy requires urgent treatment of severe-range pressure using pregnancy-compatible agents. Avoid treating the early percentage as a mandatory minimum reduction in every patient. A patient whose perfusion worsens needs immediate reassessment of the target, drug effect and underlying diagnosis. Once stabilized, transition carefully to a long-acting oral regimen rather than allowing infusion withdrawal to produce recurrent uncontrolled pressure.

Lower SBP directly to 130–139 mmHg and maintain that range for the first week: A narrow acute systolic range is used in a defined spontaneous-ICH pathway in the 2025 hypertension guideline. It should not be transferred to an unspecified nonstroke emergency.

Reduce SBP to below 120 mmHg immediately and maintain heart rate at 60–80/min: This resembles an acute aortic anti-impulse target when perfusion permits. It is not the default pressure schedule for every hypertensive emergency.

Allow the pressure to remain unchanged initially and reduce it about 15% over the first day: A cautious first-day approach can apply to selected ischemic-stroke patients without reperfusion treatment or another compelling indication. It is not the general strategy for ongoing acute hypertension-related organ injury.

AHA/ACC high blood pressure guideline, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001356

questions.question: A patient with hypertensive encephalopathy needs a titratable IV infusion. Heart rate is 48/min, there is active bronchospasm and eGFR is 19 mL/min/1.73 m². There is no advanced aortic stenosis or acute pulmonary edema. Which listed drug best fits?
options: Nicardipine
Labetalol
Sodium nitroprusside
Hydralazine
questions.explanation:
Selecting Nicardipine in Hypertensive Encephalopathy

Correct answer: Nicardipine

Drug Selection

**Nicardipine lowers vascular resistance without relying on beta blockade or AV-nodal suppression.** It is a useful titratable option for neurological hypertensive emergencies when the clinical profile permits.

A common IV regimen starts at ==5 mg/hour== and increases by ==2.5 mg/hour== at about five-minute intervals to a maximum of ==15 mg/hour==, with adjustment according to response and local protocol.

Check the full presentation before choosing it. Advanced aortic stenosis is a contraindication in the cited hypertension table, and acute aortic syndromes require an anti-impulse strategy rather than vasodilator-first treatment.

Monitoring and Differential Diagnosis

**Follow pressure and neurological function while avoiding an excessive early fall.** Tachycardia, headache, local infusion problems and hypotension are relevant adverse effects.

An encephalopathic presentation needs evaluation for ICH, ischemic stroke, seizures, toxic/metabolic disorders and other competing causes. A posterior vasogenic-edema pattern can support PRES but does not remove the need to identify its trigger.

The renal impairment and bradycardia are treatment-selection information, not reasons to postpone pressure control when acute injury is present. Use a monitored setting and select the target from the actual neurological diagnosis. Labetalol remains appropriate in other patients without the supplied limiting features, and nitroprusside retains selected indications where its risks can be managed. Hydralazine should not be generalized from obstetric protocols into a preferred infusion substitute for every emergency. Transition to oral therapy after stabilization and address adherence, medication exposures and the long-term BP phenotype.

Labetalol: Labetalol is useful in many hypertensive emergencies, but beta blockade is poorly matched to active bronchospasm and marked bradycardia. Those findings favor a different titratable mechanism.

Sodium nitroprusside: Nitroprusside is a potent rapidly titratable vasodilator for selected settings. Intracranial-pressure effects and metabolite accumulation with renal impairment make it less attractive than nicardipine for this neurological/renal profile.

Hydralazine: IV hydralazine has an important obstetric role and can lower pressure in selected patients. Its less predictable magnitude and duration make controlled neurological titration harder than with a short-acting infusion.

bullets.text: **Nicardipine lowers vascular resistance without relying on beta blockade or AV-nodal suppression.** It is a useful titratable option for neurological hypertensive emergencies when the clinical profile permits.
children: A common IV regimen starts at ==5 mg/hour== and increases by ==2.5 mg/hour== at about five-minute intervals to a maximum of ==15 mg/hour==, with adjustment according to response and local protocol.

Check the full presentation before choosing it. Advanced aortic stenosis is a contraindication in the cited hypertension table, and acute aortic syndromes require an anti-impulse strategy rather than vasodilator-first treatment.

bullets.text: **Follow pressure and neurological function while avoiding an excessive early fall.** Tachycardia, headache, local infusion problems and hypotension are relevant adverse effects.
children: An encephalopathic presentation needs evaluation for ICH, ischemic stroke, seizures, toxic/metabolic disorders and other competing causes. A posterior vasogenic-edema pattern can support PRES but does not remove the need to identify its trigger.

The renal impairment and bradycardia are treatment-selection information, not reasons to postpone pressure control when acute injury is present. Use a monitored setting and select the target from the actual neurological diagnosis. Labetalol remains appropriate in other patients without the supplied limiting features, and nitroprusside retains selected indications where its risks can be managed. Transition to oral therapy after stabilization and address adherence, medication exposures and the long-term BP phenotype.

questions.question: A patient has BP 232/136 mmHg, confusion, platelets 16 × 10⁹/L, schistocytes, undetectable haptoglobin and creatinine 1.6 mg/dL. MCV is 86 fL and INR 1.0; there is no cancer or transplant history. ADAMTS13 samples have been collected. Which next approach is best?
options: Start urgent plasma exchange and corticosteroids while controlling BP
Control BP alone while awaiting ADAMTS13 results
Perform kidney biopsy before starting TTP-directed treatment
Start complement inhibition as the initial etiological treatment
questions.explanation:
Severe Hypertension With Thrombotic Microangiopathy

Correct answer: Start urgent plasma exchange and corticosteroids while controlling BP

Differential Diagnosis

**Severe pressure does not exclude TTP.** Hypertension-associated TMA, immune TTP, complement-mediated TMA, pregnancy-related syndromes and other secondary causes can overlap clinically.

The supplied findings give a PLASMIC score of seven, a high-risk pattern for severe ADAMTS13 deficiency. Scores of 0–4 are low risk, five intermediate and 6–7 high; the score does not replace an assay or clinical judgment.

ADAMTS13 activity below ==10%== strongly supports TTP in the appropriate setting. Collect activity and inhibitor/antibody samples before plasma therapy when possible, without delaying urgent treatment.

Immediate Management

**Treat the pressure-related organ injury and the suspected hematological emergency in parallel.** ISTH guidance supports urgent therapeutic plasma exchange and corticosteroids when TTP probability is high, before a delayed ADAMTS13 result returns.

One published expert protocol uses daily replacement of 1–1.5 plasma volumes and IV methylprednisolone ==1 mg/kg== after exchange. Hematology individualizes the protocol and early caplacizumab/rituximab decisions. The 2025 update preserves acute immune-TTP recommendations; recombinant ADAMTS13 prevention in congenital TTP is a separate indication.

Reassess the diagnosis when assay results and the clinical response become available. A renal-predominant TMA with no severe ADAMTS13 deficiency may require a different pathway, including evaluation for complement-mediated disease. Improvement after pressure control can support hypertension-associated injury, but waiting for that improvement is not a safe initial diagnostic test in this high-risk presentation. Follow neurological status, hemolysis, platelet trend, renal function and bleeding risk, and coordinate medication and procedure decisions across the critical-care and hematology teams.

PLASMIC item: 1 point each | Criterion

Platelets | <30 × 10⁹/L

Hemolysis | Reticulocytes ==>2.5%==, undetectable haptoglobin or indirect bilirubin ==>2 mg/dL==

Cancer | No active cancer in the preceding year

Transplant | No solid-organ or hematopoietic stem-cell transplant

MCV | <90 fL

INR | <1.5

Creatinine | ==<2 mg/dL==

Control BP alone while awaiting ADAMTS13 results: Severe hypertension can itself cause TMA, but profound thrombocytopenia, hemolysis and this high-probability clinical profile raise concern for TTP. Waiting for a delayed assay without TTP-directed assessment and treatment can be dangerous.

Perform kidney biopsy before starting TTP-directed treatment: Biopsy can help selected unresolved renal TMA presentations. It is not a prerequisite to urgent treatment of probable TTP and is particularly problematic with profound thrombocytopenia.

Start complement inhibition as the initial etiological treatment: Complement inhibition is appropriate for selected complement-mediated TMA after expert assessment. The supplied high-likelihood severe-ADAMTS13-deficiency profile requires immediate consideration of TTP rather than an unqualified assumption of complement-mediated disease.

questions.question: A patient hospitalized for cellulitis has repeated BP 212/116 mmHg after missing home antihypertensives. There are no ischemic, neurological or respiratory symptoms; examination and directed testing show no acute organ injury. What is the best BP approach?
options: Give repeated as-needed IV labetalol doses to normalize the reading
Start a nicardipine infusion until BP is below 160/100 mmHg
Reinstitute an appropriate scheduled oral regimen and arrange timely reassessment
Give repeated short-acting oral doses until a discharge pressure target is reached
questions.explanation:
Severe Asymptomatic Inpatient BP Without Acute Injury

Correct answer: Reinstitute an appropriate scheduled oral regimen and arrange timely reassessment

Clinical Assessment

**Confirm the measurement and look for acute injury before selecting the urgency of treatment.** Review missed doses, pain, anxiety, sleep disruption, withdrawal, fluid balance and medicines such as NSAIDs or sympathomimetics.

Symptoms and examination guide additional tests. A high value should not be dismissed without assessment, but chronic LVH or stable CKD is not the same as new acute injury.

AHA/ACC 2025 specifically discourages intermittent additional IV or oral drugs used to acutely lower severe pressure in patients hospitalized for noncardiac conditions without acute target-organ damage.

Treatment and Follow-Up

**Restore durable control rather than chase immediate normalization.** Reinstitute a suitable home regimen or initiate/intensify scheduled oral treatment after checking the clinical context and relevant renal/electrolyte status.

Address access and adherence, explain how to monitor at home and arrange timely review. A patient with unreliable follow-up or concerning clinical evolution may need a different observation or care plan.

Do not use an infusion or repeated rescue doses simply to satisfy a numerical discharge threshold. At the same time, avoid sending the patient away with no treatment plan or assuming that an asymptomatic episode implies low long-term risk. Repeat assessment if chest pain, dyspnea, neurological findings or acute kidney deterioration appears. The distinction is between a chronic-control problem requiring prompt organized care and an acute organ syndrome requiring emergency reduction; the pressure reading alone does not identify which situation is present.

Perioperative Distinctions

**Perioperative decisions consider surgical risk and clinical context, not a universal cancellation number.** AHA/ACC 2024 allows considering deferral for elective elevated-risk surgery in patients with cardiovascular risk factors and recent poorly controlled BP at least ==180 mmHg== systolic or ==110 mmHg== diastolic before the day of surgery.

Continue established beta blockers when clinically appropriate; avoid starting one on the day of surgery without an immediate indication. For selected patients taking a RAS inhibitor for controlled hypertension before elevated-risk noncardiac surgery, omission 24 hours beforehand may limit intraoperative hypotension. Continuation is reasonable when the indication is HFrEF.

Coordinate withholding and restart with anesthesia and the treating team. Treat pain, hypoxia, retention and withdrawal states; do not confuse individualized perioperative management with an indication for reflex rescue treatment of every asymptomatic ward elevation.

Give repeated as-needed IV labetalol doses to normalize the reading: IV labetalol has emergency indications, but intermittent treatment of an isolated inpatient elevation without acute injury can create large pressure swings and hypotension without a demonstrated clinical benefit.

Start a nicardipine infusion until BP is below 160/100 mmHg: A titratable infusion is appropriate when an acute organ-injury syndrome requires monitored lowering. It is not justified solely by this asymptomatic inpatient number and can produce excessive reduction.

Give repeated short-acting oral doses until a discharge pressure target is reached: An appropriate oral regimen may need initiation or adjustment, but repeated rescue dosing to force a number is different from planned sustained treatment. Delayed drug effects can stack and cause hypotension after the immediate observation period.

questions.question: CT confirms an acute aortic dissection in a patient with BP 218/122 mmHg and sinus rate 124/min. There is no shock or severe acute aortic regurgitation. Which listed IV drug should generally be initiated first?
options: Enalaprilat
Nicardipine
Sodium nitroprusside
Esmolol
questions.explanation:
Acute Aortic Syndrome: Initial Anti-Impulse Therapy

Correct answer: Esmolol

Anti-Impulse Targets

**Initial beta blockade reduces heart rate and the force of ventricular ejection before additional vasodilation.** The 2022 ACC/AHA aortic guidance targets heart rate 60–80/min and systolic pressure below ==120 mmHg==, or the lowest pressure that preserves adequate organ perfusion.

Esmolol is useful because its short duration permits rapid adjustment. A common regimen uses a ==500 µg/kg== loading dose over one minute followed by ==50 µg/kg/min==, titrated under close monitoring; modify or omit a loading dose when the clinical state warrants.

Add a titratable vasodilator if BP remains above the appropriate target after impulse control. Provide analgesia and urgent aortic-team assessment; medication does not replace definitive management.

Contraindications and Escalation

**Preserve perfusion while treating wall stress.** Evaluate malperfusion, tamponade, rupture and severe acute regurgitation because those complications can change the immediate strategy.

When beta blockade is contraindicated or not tolerated, an IV nondihydropyridine CCB may be considered for rate control if the ventricular and conduction profile permits. Do not treat it as interchangeable in decompensated HFrEF or important conduction disease.

Type A dissection generally requires emergency surgical management, while type B care depends on complications and anatomy. Continue frequent neurological, limb, renal and pressure reassessment. A generic gradual twenty-four-hour hypertension schedule is insufficient for an otherwise stable acute aortic syndrome requiring rapid impulse control. Conversely, forcing a nominal target despite new shock or malperfusion is unsafe. The question therefore specifies the absence of important contraindications and asks about the initial agent, not whether a vasodilator will eventually be needed.

Enalaprilat: IV ACE inhibition can lower pressure in selected circumstances, but its less readily titratable response does not provide the immediate anti-impulse control needed in this tachycardic aortic syndrome.

Nicardipine: Nicardipine can be added if pressure remains high after adequate rate/impulse control. Starting a vasodilator first can provoke reflex tachycardia and increase aortic wall stress.

Sodium nitroprusside: Nitroprusside can provide additional rapid pressure control in selected monitored patients. It should not replace the initial control of heart rate and contractile impulse when beta blockade is appropriate.

questions.question: A patient with chronic hypertension develops pulmonary edema over minutes, with BP 228/132 mmHg and oxygen saturation 82%. Weight is unchanged from a recent clinic visit, there is no leg edema and LVEF is 60%. Which predominant mechanism best explains this presentation?
options: Abrupt afterload elevation with increased LV filling pressure and fluid redistribution
Gradual extracellular-volume expansion from renal sodium retention
Primary alveolar-capillary permeability injury
Reduced plasma oncotic pressure from substantial protein loss
questions.explanation:
Pressure-Driven Pulmonary Edema and Fluid Redistribution

Correct answer: Abrupt afterload elevation with increased LV filling pressure and fluid redistribution

Pathophysiology and Immediate Treatment

**Severe afterload elevation can abruptly increase left-sided filling pressure and redistribute fluid into the lungs.** Total-body volume excess is not required to produce dramatic pulmonary edema.

Provide oxygen for hypoxemia and use CPAP or bilevel support early when appropriate. Assess mental state, airway protection and response; deteriorating respiratory failure may require intubation.

Preserved EF does not exclude severely elevated filling pressure or acute cardiac pulmonary edema. IV nitroglycerin can reduce filling pressure and arterial load when appropriate: a conventional infusion starts at ==5–10 µg/min==, increasing by ==5–10 µg/min== every three to five minutes. A common range is ==10–200 µg/min==; selected severe presentations use more intensive monitored protocols.

Monitoring and Additional Treatment

**Follow respiratory effort, oxygenation, BP and perfusion together.** A reduction in the displayed pressure is not sufficient if oxygenation or clinical work of breathing continues to worsen.

Add an appropriate IV loop diuretic when congestion and volume excess warrant it, using previous diuretic exposure and renal function to guide dosing. Identify ischemia, arrhythmia, valve failure and medication interruption as possible precipitants.

Avoid nitrates with relevant PDE-5 inhibitor exposure and use caution in preload-dependent states. Do not initiate beta blockade simply to treat the acute pressure during overt decompensated pulmonary edema. More intensive nitrate protocols are used in selected severe cases, but a specific high-dose bolus is not a universal requirement. Transition to durable treatment after stabilization and reassess the cardiac phenotype. Mechanism-directed care combines respiratory support and rapid filling-pressure relief with assessment of the actual volume excess.

Gradual extracellular-volume expansion from renal sodium retention: Renal sodium retention can cause cardiogenic congestion, especially with CKD or missed dialysis, and may coexist with pressure elevation. The very rapid presentation without recent weight gain favors redistribution and afterload mismatch as the immediate dominant mechanism.

Primary alveolar-capillary permeability injury: Permeability edema occurs in settings such as sepsis, aspiration or inhalational injury and can cause severe hypoxemia. Marked pressure elevation and this rapid cardiac filling-pressure phenotype favor a hydrostatic mechanism; preserved EF does not exclude it.

Reduced plasma oncotic pressure from substantial protein loss: Hypoalbuminemia can contribute to edema in nephrotic or other protein-losing states. It is less suited to explaining a minute-scale hypertensive pulmonary presentation without peripheral edema or a stated protein-losing disorder.

questions.explanationHtml:
Pressure-Driven Pulmonary Edema and Fluid Redistribution

Correct answer: A — Abrupt afterload elevation with increased LV filling pressure and fluid redistribution

Pathophysiology and Immediate Treatment

  • Severe afterload elevation can abruptly increase left-sided filling pressure and redistribute fluid into the lungs. Total-body volume excess is not required to produce dramatic pulmonary edema.
    • Provide oxygen for hypoxemia and use CPAP or bilevel support early when appropriate. Assess mental state, airway protection and response; deteriorating respiratory failure may require intubation.
    • Preserved EF does not exclude severely elevated filling pressure or acute cardiac pulmonary edema. IV nitroglycerin can reduce filling pressure and arterial load when appropriate: a conventional infusion starts at 5–10 µg/min, increasing by 5–10 µg/min every three to five minutes. A common range is 10–200 µg/min; selected severe presentations use more intensive monitored protocols.

Monitoring and Additional Treatment

  • Follow respiratory effort, oxygenation, BP and perfusion together. A reduction in the displayed pressure is not sufficient if oxygenation or clinical work of breathing continues to worsen.
    • Add an appropriate IV loop diuretic when congestion and volume excess warrant it, using previous diuretic exposure and renal function to guide dosing. Identify ischemia, arrhythmia, valve failure and medication interruption as possible precipitants.
    • Avoid nitrates with relevant PDE-5 inhibitor exposure and use caution in preload-dependent states. Do not initiate beta blockade simply to treat the acute pressure during overt decompensated pulmonary edema. More intensive nitrate protocols are used in selected severe cases, but a specific high-dose bolus is not a universal requirement. Transition to durable treatment after stabilization and reassess the cardiac phenotype. Mechanism-directed care combines respiratory support and rapid filling-pressure relief with assessment of the actual volume excess.

Other Options

  • B — Gradual extracellular-volume expansion from renal sodium retention: Renal sodium retention can cause cardiogenic congestion, especially with CKD or missed dialysis, and may coexist with pressure elevation. The very rapid presentation without recent weight gain favors redistribution and afterload mismatch as the immediate dominant mechanism.
  • C — Primary alveolar-capillary permeability injury: Permeability edema occurs in settings such as sepsis, aspiration or inhalational injury and can cause severe hypoxemia. Marked pressure elevation and this rapid cardiac filling-pressure phenotype favor a hydrostatic mechanism; preserved EF does not exclude it.
  • D — Reduced plasma oncotic pressure from substantial protein loss: Hypoalbuminemia can contribute to edema in nephrotic or other protein-losing states. It is less suited to explaining a minute-scale hypertensive pulmonary presentation without peripheral edema or a stated protein-losing disorder.

  • AHA/ACC high blood pressure guideline, 2025

  • MSF noncommunicable disease clinical guidance, 2025

questions.question: During treatment of an acute coronary syndrome, aortic diastolic pressure falls while LV end-diastolic pressure remains elevated. Which change most directly explains why excessive pressure reduction can worsen subendocardial ischemia?
options: A fall in ventricular wall stress
A fall in the diastolic coronary perfusion gradient
A fall in myocardial oxygen demand
A fall in venous return
questions.explanation:
Coronary Perfusion During BP Treatment in Acute Ischemia

Correct answer: A fall in the diastolic coronary perfusion gradient

Coronary Perfusion Physiology

**Left-ventricular subendocardial perfusion occurs predominantly during diastole.** A useful approximation of its driving gradient is aortic diastolic pressure minus LV end-diastolic pressure.

When aortic diastolic pressure falls and LVEDP stays high, the gradient narrows. Tachycardia can compound the problem by shortening diastole while increasing oxygen demand.

A systolic value that appears improved therefore cannot be interpreted separately from diastolic pressure, filling pressure, heart rate and signs of organ perfusion.

Treatment of Hypertensive Coronary Ischemia

**Treat ischemia and arrange the indicated coronary strategy while lowering pressure in a controlled manner.** Nitroglycerin can relieve symptoms and reduce preload/afterload when there is no contraindication.

A titratable beta blocker can be useful with tachycardia and adequate perfusion, but not when shock risk, acute decompensated HF, important bradycardia, AV block or another contraindication changes the balance.

Avoid unnecessary rapid reduction that produces hypotension or worsens coronary supply. Reassess chest pain, ECG changes, pulse, respiratory status and the need for urgent reperfusion rather than attributing persistent ischemia to a pressure number alone. Nitrate safety also depends on recent PDE-5 inhibitor exposure and whether the patient is preload dependent, as in selected right-ventricular infarction presentations. There is no single low diastolic target that should be forced in every ACS patient. Long-term outpatient BP goals and the immediate management of ischemic perfusion are related but distinct decisions.

A fall in ventricular wall stress: Reduced afterload and wall stress generally lower myocardial oxygen demand and can be beneficial. They do not explain the loss of driving pressure for coronary flow when aortic diastolic pressure falls excessively.

A fall in myocardial oxygen demand: Lower demand is an intended anti-ischemic treatment effect. Ischemia can nevertheless worsen if the reduction in oxygen supply from impaired perfusion outweighs that benefit.

A fall in venous return: Reduced venous return can relieve congestion but can be harmful in a preload-dependent presentation. The supplied combination of low aortic diastolic pressure and persistently high LV filling pressure specifically identifies a coronary driving-gradient problem.

AHA/ACC high blood pressure guideline, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001356

ESC elevated blood pressure and hypertension guideline, 2024 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehae178

questions.question: A noncomatose patient with a mild-to-moderate spontaneous ICH presents within six hours with SBP 192 mmHg. Under the AHA/ACC 2025 hypertension recommendation, which acute systolic range is appropriate if tolerated?
options: 130 to below 140 mmHg
110 to below 120 mmHg
140 to below 150 mmHg
160 to below 180 mmHg
questions.explanation:
Acute BP Control in Spontaneous Intracerebral Hemorrhage

Correct answer: 130 to below 140 mmHg

Eligibility and Target

**AHA/ACC 2025 supports prompt lowering to systolic 130 to below ==140 mmHg== in the selected spontaneous-ICH population presenting at ==150–220 mmHg==.** The recommendation specifies maintaining treatment for at least seven days, with antihypertensive treatment stopped if SBP falls below 130.

Use smooth, sustained control with a rapidly titratable drug and minimize variability. Nicardipine is one practical option when its contraindications are absent.

The 2022 dedicated ICH guidance described an initial target of 140 with maintenance at 130–150 for mild-to-moderate disease. Do not silently merge that wording with the later hypertension recommendation.

Monitoring and Limitations

**Apply the evidence to the stated severity and presentation.** Large or severe hemorrhage, important intracranial-pressure problems and a need for emergency surgery require individualized neurological and critical-care assessment.

Follow neurological status, pressure trajectory, renal function and signs of inadequate perfusion. Abrupt overshoot can be harmful even when the desired target is evidence-based.

Pressure control is one part of ICH care. Address anticoagulant reversal when indicated, airway and oxygenation, hydrocephalus, neurosurgical decisions and other acute complications. A general nonstroke emergency schedule or an ischemic-stroke permissive-pressure rule is not a substitute for the ICH-specific plan. The question names the document and population so that closely related target ranges can be distinguished without implying that every patient with any intracranial bleed should receive the same regimen.

110 to below 120 mmHg: This is below the recommended acute range and risks excessive reduction. In the cited pathway, treatment should be stopped if systolic pressure falls below 130 rather than pushed toward a normal outpatient value.

140 to below 150 mmHg: The 2022 ICH guidance described targeting 140 while maintaining 130–150 in selected mild-to-moderate cases. The question specifically asks for the narrower 2025 hypertension recommendation, so the society document and year matter.

160 to below 180 mmHg: A higher range may reflect a different severity profile, a temporary state during titration or an individualized limitation. It is not the stated 2025 recommendation for this selected noncomatose, early-presenting ICH scenario.

AHA/ACC high blood pressure guideline, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001356

AHA/ASA spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage guideline, 2022 — https://doi.org/10.1161/STR.0000000000000407

questions.question: A patient with disabling acute ischemic stroke is otherwise eligible for IV thrombolysis. BP is 198/112 mmHg. Under AHA/ASA 2026, what is the specific pre-thrombolysis BP eligibility boundary?
options: SBP below 180 and DBP below 105 mmHg
SBP below 185 and DBP below 110 mmHg
SBP below 140 and DBP below 90 mmHg
SBP below 220 and DBP below 120 mmHg
questions.explanation:
Ischemic Stroke: BP Before Intravenous Thrombolysis

Correct answer: SBP below 185 and DBP below 110 mmHg

Reperfusion-Specific Thresholds

**Before IV thrombolysis, lower SBP below 185 and DBP below ==110 mmHg==.** Both components must meet the criterion, and an acceptable pressure needs to be maintained rather than documented once between recurrent spikes.

After IVT, maintain BP below ==180/105 mmHg== for at least twenty-four hours. Use a stroke-unit protocol with close pressure and neurological monitoring.

IV labetalol or a titrated nicardipine infusion can be used when appropriate; choose according to heart rate, bronchospasm, conduction and the overall clinical state. Do not use an arbitrary oral loading strategy that delays or destabilizes reperfusion planning.

Intensive Lowering and Other Stroke Pathways

**The 2026 guideline advises against assuming that lower is better after reperfusion.** Intensive systolic reduction below 140 after IVT has not improved functional outcomes in the stated mild-to-moderate population.

After successful anterior-circulation thrombectomy, a target below 140 during the first seventy-two hours is harmful and not recommended when there is no other BP-management indication. Do not generalize that statement to withholding treatment for a separate aortic or cardiac emergency.

Patients not receiving reperfusion follow a different BP pathway, often allowing substantially higher pressure unless another compelling condition is present. Correct hypotension and hypovolemia, which can compromise cerebral perfusion. Match the threshold to the treatment stage, monitor for neurological deterioration and hemorrhage, and reassess the whole reperfusion plan if pressure cannot be safely controlled. A post-treatment ceiling should not be mistaken for a more restrictive prerequisite before treatment begins.

AHA/ASA 2026 setting | BP recommendation

Before IV thrombolysis | SBP <185 AND DBP ==<110 mmHg==

After IV thrombolysis | BP ==<180/105 mmHg== for at least 24 hours

Successful anterior-circulation EVT, no other BP indication | Do not actively target SBP ==<140 mmHg== during the first 72 hours

SBP below 180 and DBP below 105 mmHg: This is the standard post-thrombolysis ceiling for at least the first twenty-four hours. It is a related but different stage-specific threshold; the pre-IVT eligibility boundary is below 185/110.

SBP below 140 and DBP below 90 mmHg: That lower pressure is not required to establish IVT eligibility. Excessive intensive lowering can delay reperfusion or impair perfusion and has not shown the assumed functional benefit in this setting.

SBP below 220 and DBP below 120 mmHg: A much more permissive threshold can be relevant to selected ischemic-stroke patients not receiving reperfusion and without another urgent BP indication. It is not the pressure criterion for IV thrombolysis.

AHA/ASA acute ischemic stroke guideline, 2026 — https://doi.org/10.1161/STR.0000000000000513

questions.question: After cocaine exposure, an agitated patient has BP 216/126 mmHg, sinus rate 142/min and marked diaphoresis. Airway and breathing are adequate. Which listed initial treatment best addresses the central hyperadrenergic state while organ injury is assessed?
options: IV nicardipine
IV phentolamine
A titrated benzodiazepine
IV nitroglycerin
questions.explanation:
Stimulant-Associated Hyperadrenergic Hypertension

Correct answer: A titrated benzodiazepine

Immediate Management

**Benzodiazepines are first-line treatment for stimulant-related agitation and hyperadrenergic activation.** Titrate in a monitored setting while assessing airway, ventilation, temperature, seizures and cardiovascular injury.

For nonseizure symptomatic cocaine toxicity, an NHS ambulance PGD illustrates diazepam ==1–2 mg== slowly IV over two minutes per increment, allowing two to five minutes between increments to titrate toward ==10 mg==. A further titrated dose may be given after ten minutes if needed, with a 20-mg episode ceiling in that protocol. This is a specific off-label protocol example; other emergency/toxicology regimens may differ.

Use ECG, glucose, electrolytes, renal assessment and other directed tests according to the presentation. Chest pain, focal neurological findings, hyperthermia or rhabdomyolysis can change the required level and type of care.

Persistent Hypertension and Ischemia

**If sedation and supportive treatment do not adequately control a hypertensive emergency, add a short-acting titratable agent matched to the organ syndrome.** Phentolamine, nitroprusside or a suitable CCB can have a role; nitrates are useful when coronary vasospasm or ischemia is relevant.

Avoid treating every stimulant presentation as if it were elective pheochromocytoma preparation. Equally, do not ignore vasoconstriction and ischemia while focusing only on the heart rate.

The beta-blocker issue requires qualification: contemporary guidance may consider agents with combined alpha/beta activity in selected circumstances when beta blockade is needed. An unqualified assertion that all beta blockers are prohibited in every patient is not a faithful summary of the evidence. Monitor ventilation and pressure during sedation, particularly with alcohol/opioid co-exposure; consult toxicology when instability persists. Assess delayed complications and arrange substance-use care after the acute episode.

IV nicardipine: A titratable CCB can be appropriate when hypertension persists or an organ-injury syndrome requires it. Pressure lowering alone does not replace management of the intoxication-related agitation and sympathetic drive.

IV phentolamine: Alpha blockade can be useful for persistent hypertension or vasoconstriction in an appropriate toxicological setting. It does not address agitation and central sympathetic activation as directly as first-line GABAergic treatment.

IV nitroglycerin: Nitroglycerin is useful for cocaine-associated ischemic symptoms or selected vasospastic/pulmonary presentations. Without replacing indicated anti-ischemic treatment, sedation is the more direct initial response to the hyperadrenergic agitation in this stem.

bullets.text: **Benzodiazepines are first-line treatment for stimulant-related agitation and hyperadrenergic activation.** Titrate in a monitored setting while assessing airway, ventilation, temperature, seizures and cardiovascular injury.
children: For nonseizure symptomatic cocaine toxicity, an NHS ambulance PGD illustrates diazepam ==1–2 mg== slowly IV over two minutes per increment, allowing two to five minutes between increments to titrate toward ==10 mg==. questions.question: At 34 weeks, a patient has repeated BP 168/112 mmHg over twenty minutes with persistent headache. Preeclampsia with severe features is being managed by the obstetric team. Which immediate strategy is best?
options: Wait for two severe readings four hours apart before beginning acute BP treatment
Give magnesium alone and reassess whether BP falls before adding an antihypertensive
Start oral methyldopa and await its full effect before changing treatment
Treat severe BP promptly with a first-line rapid agent and give magnesium for seizure prophylaxis
questions.explanation:
Management of Severe Hypertension in Pregnancy

Correct answer: Treat severe BP promptly with a first-line rapid agent and give magnesium for seizure prophylaxis

Threshold and Timing

**Persistent SBP at least 160 or DBP at least ==110 mmHg== in pregnancy or postpartum requires urgent treatment.** ACOG describes persistence for at least fifteen minutes and treatment as soon as possible within thirty to sixty minutes of confirmation.

First-line rapid options include IV labetalol, IV hydralazine or immediate-release oral nifedipine when appropriate. Choice depends on access, heart rate, asthma and other clinical factors.

Illustrative initial doses include labetalol ==20 mg== IV with reassessment and protocol-based escalation, hydralazine ==5–10 mg== IV, or nifedipine ==10–20 mg== orally with repeat assessment at about twenty minutes. Use a defined obstetric protocol rather than combining parts of different escalation schedules.

Seizure Prophylaxis and Monitoring

**Magnesium sulfate addresses seizure risk independently of the BP drug.** For example, the SOMANZ 2023 IV regimen uses ==4 g== over twenty minutes followed by ==1 g/hour==, continued until twenty-four hours after delivery or the last seizure, whichever is later. Apply the indicated renal adjustments and local obstetric protocol.

Monitor respiratory rate, tendon reflexes, urine output and clinical state. Renal impairment increases accumulation risk. For suspected toxicity, stop the infusion, support ventilation and follow the antidote protocol; SOMANZ describes calcium gluconate ==1 g== IV, given as 10 mL of ==10%== solution diluted and infused over ten minutes.

Continue the obstetric assessment of platelet count, liver and kidney injury, fetal status and timing of delivery. A pressure response does not establish that severe preeclampsia has resolved. Conversely, a magnesium infusion does not demonstrate that the maternal stroke risk from severe hypertension has been addressed. The same urgent pressure principles apply postpartum, when severe disease can appear after delivery. Stabilization, seizure prevention and delivery planning are coordinated clinical tasks rather than alternative competing treatments.

Wait for two severe readings four hours apart before beginning acute BP treatment: A four-hour interval is used in some nonsevere diagnostic definitions. Persistent severe pressure is confirmed over minutes so treatment is not delayed for hours.

Give magnesium alone and reassess whether BP falls before adding an antihypertensive: Magnesium prevents or treats eclamptic seizures; it is not a substitute for urgent treatment of persistent severe pressure. Both problems need an appropriate parallel plan.

Start oral methyldopa and await its full effect before changing treatment: Methyldopa can be used for selected ongoing pregnancy BP management. Its slower action does not fit the time-critical treatment of persistent severe-range pressure.

questions.question: At ten weeks of pregnancy, a patient with chronic hypertension has BP averaging 152/96 mmHg while taking losartan. There is active asthma requiring bronchodilator treatment, but no acute organ injury. Which listed ongoing regimen best fits?
options: Stop losartan and use methyldopa
Stop losartan and use labetalol
Stop losartan and use extended-release nifedipine
Stop losartan and use oral hydralazine alone
questions.explanation:
Ongoing Hypertension Treatment During Pregnancy

Correct answer: Stop losartan and use extended-release nifedipine

Drug Selection

**ACE inhibitors and ARBs should be replaced with a pregnancy-compatible regimen.** Do not continue losartan until later pregnancy simply because the patient is currently in the first trimester.

Extended-release nifedipine and labetalol are preferred first-line ongoing agents in current American guidance. The asthma history makes nifedipine the better listed choice; the extended-release preparation is for maintenance and is not interchangeable with an acute immediate-release protocol.

A usual nifedipine ER starting dose is ==30 mg== daily, titrated according to response up to a typical maximum of ==120 mg==/day. Monitor headache, flushing, edema, pressure and symptoms during adjustment.

Targets and Follow-Up

**Chronic pregnancy hypertension has a lower treatment threshold than an acute severe-range emergency.** Current CHAP-informed care supports initiating or titrating treatment from ==140/90 mmHg== rather than waiting for 160/110.

An acute severe reading still requires the urgent pathway, while this stable average calls for a supervised ongoing plan. Arrange obstetric follow-up and assessment for superimposed preeclampsia when symptoms, laboratory findings or the pressure trajectory suggest it.

A labetalol maintenance regimen commonly begins at ==100–200 mg== twice daily when there is no limiting asthma, bradycardia or cardiac contraindication. Methyldopa remains an alternative when preferred options cannot be used. Discuss all medicines, fetal considerations and adherence, and reassess the regimen postpartum because lactation and nonpregnant drug choices differ from pregnancy restrictions. Avoid describing a drug as universally unsafe during breastfeeding simply because it is avoided during pregnancy. Durable control and surveillance protect against progression while preserving the distinction between routine titration and emergency treatment.

Stop losartan and use methyldopa: Methyldopa is a pregnancy-compatible alternative, but is often less effective or less well tolerated because of sedation and other adverse effects. Extended-release nifedipine is a preferred first-line option in this clinical profile.

Stop losartan and use labetalol: Labetalol is a preferred pregnancy agent in an appropriate patient. Active bronchospastic disease is an important reason to choose the other preferred first-line option offered here.

Stop losartan and use oral hydralazine alone: Hydralazine has selected uses, particularly IV treatment of severe pregnancy hypertension or later-line chronic combinations. Oral hydralazine monotherapy is less attractive than the preferred long-acting option for sustained control.
